speechtext: What is being done by the government to assist secondary industries in Newfoundland?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question, standing in the name of the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins), appeared on yesterday's order paper. For some reason that is not apparent, it does not appear on today's order paper. It was not answered yesterday, but the answer is available today and is as follows:
In accordance with the terms of union, the interdepartmental committee on Newfoundland secondary industries and purchasing was established in January of this year. It is comprised of representatives

from eleven federal departments and agencies, and was given the task of (a) stimulating the purchasing of federal government supplies and services from Newfoundland secondary industries; (b) providing Newfoundland industries with a clearing house to which particular problems can be directed; (c) acting in an advisory capacity to the government in dealing with problems of these industries.
An office is also being maintained in St. John's, Newfoundland, by the Department of Trade and Commerce for the purpose of giving Newfoundland businessmen information and advice. Through this office local manufacturers can directly place their inquiries with the committee in Ottawa.
Local purchasing offices of the Department of Transport and the Canadian Commercial Corporation have also been set up in St. John's for the purpose of contracting for local requirements. The Department of Public Works and the king's printer have made special arrangements for the purchase of supplies, stationery and printing. The co-operation of the C.N.R., particularly with regard to placing orders for stationery and printing in Newfoundland, has also been assured.
The United Nail and Foundry, which is unable to obtain its full requirements in nail rod from Canadian mills, is being paid an equalizing subsidy on rod purchased in the United States. Payments to date amount to $6,651.88. Dawes Nail and Hardware was asked to make a submission for similar treatment, but none was received.
Newfoundland manufacturers receive invitations from the federal government in Ottawa to tender on materials that may be required throughout Canada. It was apparent in the latter cases that some of the Newfoundland industries would be temporarily handicapped in competing with mainland manufacturers. The government, therefore, recently directed its purchasing authorities to place contracts with Newfoundland manufacturers whose tenders are within fifteen per cent of the lowest bid. This measure is to apply until March 31, 1950.
The government has been disappointed in the number of tenders submitted by Newfoundland manufacturers. It should be emphasized that small industries in Newfoundland must use their own initiative in finding a solution to their difficulties. The government is anxious to assist them in every way, and will give sympathetic hearing to specific remedies which they may put forward.

The house resumed, from Thursday, October 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. St. Laurent for an address to His Majesty the King praying that a measure be laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom to amend the British North America Act, 1867, relating to the amendment of the constitution of Canada, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Knowles, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Garson.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I intend to discuss the proposal for the amendment of the Bi'itish North America Act from the point of view of Canadians who live on the Pacific slope.
The province of British Columbia entered confederation in 1871 by an agreement between the young Dominion of Canada, then just four years old, and the crown colony of British Columbia. That agreement was contained in addresses to the queen passed by the parliament of Canada and by the legislature of the colony. Members who are interested may refer to page 77 of volume V of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927.
Some of the terms of the agreement are still of considerable interest. One had to do with the construction of a railway to the west coast of Canada. The paragraph dealing with the railway reads as follows:
The government of the dominion undertake to secure the commencement simultaneously, within two years from the date of the union, of the construction of a railway from the Pacific towards the Rocky mountains, and from such point as may be selected, east of the Rocky mountains, towards the Pacific, to connect the seaboard of British Columbia with the railway system of Canada; and further, to secure the completion of such railway within ten years from the date of the union.
The railway was not built within the ten years; as hon. members know, it was finally completed in 1885.

There is another interesting provision having to do with transportation, as follows:
The dominion will provide an efficient mail service, fortnightly, by steam communication between Victoria and San Francisco, and twice a week between Victoria and Olympia;-
Olympia is now the capital of the state of Washington.
-the vessels to be adapted for the conveyance of freight and passengers.
There was also provision for the payment of subsidies to the province of British Columbia. It is interesting to note that at that time the population of the province was estimated at 60,000, some 34,000 less than that of Prince Edward Island. It has increased twenty times, now almost 1,200,000. Provision also was made for the province to give large areas of land to the dominion, known as railway lands, the purpose being to further the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway.
There is also the following provision in the agreement respecting representation in this parliament:
British Columbia shall be entitled to be represented in the Senate by three members, and by six members in the House of Commons; the representation to be increased under the provisions of the British North America Act, 1867.
The colony accepted the British North America Act of that time; in other words the basis of the union was the British North America Act as it stood in 1867. Right from the start British Columbia has been the province most remote from Ottawa. I dare say half the present members of this house have never been in that province. The Prime Minister had not been there until 1948.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: He had good results after he went there, though.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
He may not have such good results the next time. Largely because of its remoteness from the capital, the problems of British Columbia have always been the least understood of those of all the provinces. Of necessity, therefore, we must always be on guard against undue centralization of power in Ottawa.
In the past our rights have been protected largely in two ways. In the first place the British North America Act has been interpreted by the decisions of a court which we have regarded as impartial, and by and large those decisions have favoured the provinces. It is significant that when the question whether or not the dominion had the right to abolish appeals to the judicial committee of the privy council was argued in the courts, the government of British Columbia was represented by counsel to argue against that proposition. I repeat, the appeal

to the privy council has been one protection. Another has been the fact that the British North America Act could be amended-at least so we thought-only after consultation and the most careful deliberation.
Protection for our province is most important, and it is now being removed by doing away with appeal to the privy council and changing the method of amending the British North America Act. These changes may prove detrimental to our province. I hope that will not be so, but there is a real possibility that we may find ourselves in that position. Regardless of the party to which we in British Columbia belong, we have always believed there would be a conference between the dominion and the provinces before any request was made for amendments to the British North America Act. It is significant to note the attitude taken by the attorney general of British Columbia -who, by the way, is a supporter of the Liberal party-when the speech from the throne appeared in the press last September. I have here a dispatch which appeared in the Vancouver Sun under date of September 16, 1949, giving the reaction of Mr. Wismer to the suggestions with respect to amending Canada's constitution. The heading reads, "Wismer approves Ottawa conference." The article goes on:
Prime Minister St. Laurent's plan to have the Canadian constitution amended at home, rather than by reference to the British parliament, drew favourable comment here today from Attorney General Gordon Wismer.
Mr. Wismer made it clear that he could not as yet speak for the provincial government as a whole, since the cabinet has not considered the national government's proposal.
This is the part of the statement I wish to emphasize.
He stressed that in any plan for altering the constitution within Canada, adequate provision must be laid down for safeguarding provincial rights.
British Columbia has long been a strong fighter for provincial rights against encroachment by the federal authority.
And, he said, he would presume that even in any changes touching federal matters alone, it would be provided that the provinces should be consulted first.
Actually that was the program of the Prime Minister before the house sat, namely, that the provinces would be consulted before any attempt would be made to amend the constitution. We find that clearly set out in the letter from the Prime Minister to the provincial premiers, which appears at page 870 of Hansard. The paragraph dealing with the Prime Minister's statement to the electorate of Canada reads:
I stated also that it was the intention of the government, after the election, to consult the provincial governments with a view to working out
British North America Act a method of amending the constitution in Canada which would be satisfactory to all Canadians.
I believe that is the program that should have been followed. Had the Prime Minister done as he said he was going to do, there could have been little quarrel with his actions. But that is not what the Prime Minister is doing in the resolution now under discussion.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: And what the hon. member has cited is not all the Prime Minister said about it, either, in the letter from which the hon. member quoted.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: The Prime Minister may speak again in this debate, but I defy him to show me and the house anything in his letter stating that his election pledge was that he would make certain amendments without consulting the provinces. There is not one word to that effect in his letter.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: Don't try to speak for the Prime Minister; you are not capable of it.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
I repeat that the resolution now under debate is not the plan the Prime Minister announced to the people. He says now that eventually he will consult the provinces, but first he is going to get certain powers to amend Canada's constitution. The Prime Minister is going to ask the government of the United Kingdom to amend the British North America Act to give the dominion power to amend the constitution, except- first-as regards matters coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the province. The second exception is as follows:
-or as regards rights or privileges by this or any other constitutional act granted or secured to the legislature or the government of a province.
By the way, Mr. Speaker, as I read this resolution, this second exception is tied up with educational and language rights. I take it from the speeches made by the Prime Minister that that was not the intention, but clearly that is the way the resolution reads. If it was not intended to restrict these provincial rights to education and language, then further words should have been added to the resolution. The part of the resolution with which I am dealing reads as follows:
-or as regards rights or privileges by this or any other constitutional act granted or secured to the legislature or the government of a province, or to any class of persons with respect to schools or as regards the use of the English or the French language.

British North America Act
If it was intended that these should be separate exceptions, I suggest to the Prime Minister he should have inserted the words "or granted or secured" before the words "to any class of persons with respect to schools or as regards the use of the English or the French language." In any event, as I understand it, the second exception is this general one:
-rights or privileges by this or any other constitutional act granted or secured to the legislature or the government of a province . . .
The third exception concerns schools and the use of the French and the English language. Those were the exceptions contained in the resolution as it was originally presented.
As the result of an amendment moved by the C.C.F. party, the Prime Minister added two more exceptions, one being that the dominion was not asking for the power to change the provision in the constitution which calls for a session of parliament once every year or the provision which calls for an election every five years. He made a proviso to the fifth exception that, in the event of real or apprehended war, an election could be postponed beyond the five-year period unless one-third of the members objected. I do not think very careful consideration was given to this proviso, because it means that with the house constituted as it is the Liberal members could extend the life of the parliament for more than five years, and the opposition parties, even though they combined, would be helpless to prevent it.
This resolution can easily, of course, be forced through this house; and I have no doubt that it will be. It will then be accepted by an obedient Senate, and the United Kingdom government will pass the amendment in the form requested by this parliament.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: Order. I do not think the hon. member should refer to the other place as the "obedient Senate."

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
I shall substitute the word "Liberal" for the word ''obedient". The United Kingdom government will pass the amendment in the form in which it is requested by this parliament, and the dominion will then have the power it seeks in this resolution, before having consulted with the provinces.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the members of this house, that the folly-I repeat that word-the folly of this postelection program of the Prime Minister's is clearly shown in several ways. In the first place, the main argument he submits is that he is bringing the Canadian constitution home, and that he is removing one of the

last badges of colonialism. In the Montreal press of October 14 the Prime Minister is reported as having said:
Now, he said, was the time to remove the "final badges of our former dependent condition."
This main argument advanced by the Prime Minister is nothing more or less than a spurious argument, because he is still leaving large parts of our constitution with the United Kingdom government. More is being left with the United Kingdom government than when the resolution was first presented, because the government has accepted the C.C.F. amendment. Yet, while doing this, the Prime Minister has also actually had the temerity to argue that he is taking no more power than he already possesses.
In his letter to Mr. Duplessis, which will be found at page 874 of Hansard, we find this statement:
We believe we already have the right to have such amendments made without consulting the provincial authorities,-
Actually the plan now being followed probably makes more remote than it would otherwise have been, the time when Canada will not have to go to the United Kingdom for an amendment to her constitution.
The folly of this post-election program is shown also by the fact that the provinces are being deprived of the right to be heard upon certain matters which, while exclusively federal under the British North America Act, actually concern the provinces. For instance, consider the composition of the Senate. One of the main reasons for having a Senate in our parliamentary structure was to protect provincial as well as minority rights. For example, Quebec and Ontario have equal representation in the Senate, although their populations differ. The maritime provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick each have ten senators, whereas the province of British Columbia, with practically twice the population of Nova Scotia and certainly more than twice the population of New Brunswick, has only six. By the way, that is a most unfair situation.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
The composition of the Senate is a matter which vitally affects all the provinces. It may be that some members of the Senate should be appointed by provincial governments. Personally I believe some arrangement of that kind would be a good thing. The point I am emphasizing is this: By this amendment the provinces are being deprived of the right to be heard on some of these questions which, under the British North America Act, would appear to be purely federal.
The folly of the program is also shown by the attitude of the various provincial

governments, and their attitude is extremely important. We need only to look at the letters written by the premiers of the various provinces to realize that many of them are in grave doubt as to the course being followed. First there is the letter from the premier of Nova Scotia, who asked that the passing of the bill abolishing appeals to the privy council be delayed until after the conference with the provinces. Then there is the letter from the premier of Quebec, in which he raises points which are clearly worthy of the most careful consideration. There is the letter from the premier of Ontario, in which he says:
I am frankly in some doubt as to the advisability of dealing with the matter piecemeal without first attempting general agreement.
There is the letter from the premier of Manitoba, in which he says:
The government of Manitoba feels that there might be differences of opinion as to whether a proposed amendment to the constitution related only to federal matters or affected provincial interests, rights, or jurisdiction. Before agreeing to any specific proposal, therefore, our government will examine carefully the manner in which the provincial position is to be protected.
Then there is the letter from the premier of Alberta, which I will not read, but which clearly sets out excellent reasons why the conference should have been held before any amendment to the act is put through.
As I said a few minutes ago, there was the immediate reaction of the attorney general of British Columbia; he said that certainly there should be a conference before any amendment was made. The premiers of Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick do not raise the question. Apparently these three Liberal premiers are taking everything on faith. But there is a most interesting letter from the premier of Saskatchewan, which is to be found in Hansard of October 24, just last Monday, at page 1107-and I hope my C.C.F. friends will be able to square this letter from the premier of Saskatchewan with the attitude they have taken in the house on this question. Mr. Douglas writes:
I must confess to considerable curiosity as to just what your government has in mind.
Further on he says:
In our opinion the field that the dominion would occupy after the suggested amendment is indefinite at the moment, and we do not know what your government has in mind in the direction of constitutional development.
Then, in connection with the Senate, he says:
Again it may be asked whether the formula would warrant the abolition of the Senate. Such an abolition would not "affect the rights and privileges of the provinces" as corporate entities; yet some of the provinces might take grave objection to the abolition of the upper chamber.
British North America Act
And he asks the Prime Minister for further clarification of the attitude of the dominion. The reply of the Prime Minister of Canada to the premier of Saskatchewan is certainly well worthy of attention. The Prime Minister uses these words:
I agree that the phrase "affecting the rights and privileges of the provinces" is lacking in precision: this general language was used because we did not wish to attempt to determine in an arbitrary fashion the extent of the rights and privileges of the provinces, preferring to leave that for determination by the courts, in the event of any dispute, unless some agreement with respect to it is reached at the forthcoming conference.
The Prime Minister himself obviously does not know just what is meant by those words "the rights and privileges of the provinces".

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
Not now. I will later, if I have time.
In effect, the provinces are being ridden over rough-shod. The field in which they may make submissions is being narrowed, and in order to prevent an invasion of any rights they may still have, they are being put in the position of having to fight before a dominion court, the Supreme Court of Canada. Premier Douglas clearly sets that out in his letter. He says:
May I make the general observation that the amendment as proposed in your letter would primarily vest in the dominion parliament authority to amend the constitution of Canada subject of course to the exceptions referred to. This would mean, as I understand the situation, that in the case of any amendment of the B.N.A. Act by the dominion being objected to by a province, the burden would be on the province to show that the amendment infringed the stated exceptions.
There is grave danger in treating the provinces in this way.
Finally, not one reason has been given for all this haste. The dominion has in view no actual amendments to the Canadian constitution. The Prime Minister explained that also in his letter to the premier of Saskatchewan, the final paragraph of which reads as follows:
As to your question whether this government "has any developments in mind which can properly be disclosed," I can only say that no consideration has yet been given by the government to any constitutional development or change which might be recommended to parliament under the new procedure contemplated by the address.
The Prime Minister gave no pledge to make an amendment without consultation with the provinces. He has no mandate to do so; yet he is forcing this resolution through now, although the conference is to be convened here in a matter of a few weeks to deal with a portion of this constitutional problem.
It all looks so unreasonable that one may well wonder about it. This action by the

British North America Act Prime Minister, on the face of it, makes one ask the question: Why is he going at it in this way? I believe that there is a good reason. I believe that the government is seeking this power at this session so that when the provinces meet here in January they will find, in the first place, that they have little power left, and, in the second place, that they can prevent an invasion in the expected fields only by fighting in the supreme court. I believe the government is of the view that at that time public opinion may well have been stirred up against the provincial premiers, thereby hampering them in their attempt to see that the provinces of Canada get fair treatment. I believe it is hoped, as a result, that the provinces will have to fall in line with the dominion proposals for dealing with the matters which are excepted in this resolution. The dominion government also hopes that the provinces will be softened up, to use a colloquial expression, for the negotiations concerning the renewal of the tax agreements, which negotiations must take place shortly. In other words I believe the hope of this government is that the provinces will find themselves looking right down the loaded barrels of two guns-one, increased power of the dominion, and the other, the fact that any disputes must be settled by a court set up by the dominion.
It is a clever, cunning, loaded-gun policy. It may work, but it is no way to promote harmony and unity in Canada. Earlier prime ministers have declined to go so far. I believe that this action of the present Prime Minister of Canada may well prove to be irresponsible, and I intend to vote against his plan.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset let it be fully understood that in common with all other members of the Social Credit group I agree that the power and the right to amend the British North America Act ought to reside in Canada. We also maintain, however, that every precaution should be taken to ensure that in Canada there shall be an unimpaired British North America Act to amend, before any Canadian agency or agencies begin to amend Canada's constitution.
Two fine old English sayings come to mind as one looks at this measure: first, don't tear down any man's house before you provide him a better one to go into; second, don't jump from the frying pan into the fire.
As I see it, passage of this measure will unhinge the British North America Act. In passing this measure it looks as though this parliament would be setting the stage for the tearing down of the Canadian people's house -its constitution, its British North America Act-before having found an acceptable plan for the construction of a new house.
There may not appear to be any sufficient reason why the present dominion government should aim to do a thing of that sort; but let it be borne in mind that the British North America Act and the Australian constitution are two of the finest constitutions in the world. The reason why they are so admirable will become manifest as I proceed. International centralizers, therefore, desire to destroy the British North America Act and the Australian constitution. I hope we do not wait too long in Canada before we come to realize that there is a body of mischievous men in the world definitely designing to

British North America Act
establish a world centralized state, in which nations like Canada and Australia will be merely minor provinces.
We live in an age of centralized totalitarian thinking, and fascist feelings are in the air everywhere. We collide with them in this house. We collide with them every time a C.C.F. member rises to speak on almost anything.
Any matter pertaining to a nation's constitution ought to be approached with the utmost gravity. In dealing with no other subject is it more important that the speaker be absolutely objective, that he seek realistically to face facts and actualities. In participating in this debate I shall do my best to be grave, realistic and honest, setting aside all possibility of prejudice.
There are many aspects of the situation confronting us at present, each of which ought to receive the most careful, cautious and appraising consideration. Every Canadian, of whatever situation in life, ought to take solemn warning that while this matter is being dealt with in this house the whole future destiny of Canadians trembles in the balance. Especially should all provincial premiers, members of provincial legislative assemblies, all municipal officials, all service clubs, all chambers of commerce, all boards of trade, all women's institutes and other women's associations, and organizations of labour-all of these should go on the alert instantly and insistently. There are exceedingly important historical scenes in progress on the Ottawa stage today.
From the point of observation from which I now view this drama it would seem to appear that particularly the premiers of the more powerful provinces might be well advised to counsel together to determine how best to manage not to leave Premier Duplessis to bear an undue measure of the burden and the brunt of needful provincial self-assertion.
May I turn to a contemplation of certain aspects of the whole general constitutional situation as it now confronts us? Everyone who has given thought to human relationships knows that the strong forever seek to impose their will upon the weak. Men have developed democracy to restrain the strong and protect the weak.
One of the secrets of successful democracy is checks and balances. Before we give too much consideration to the passing of this measure I urge upon the members of the Liberal party, whom Canadians have placed in absolute power, that they consider carefully what could easily happen to the checks and balances in relation to Canada's constitution if a certain kind of amendment should be made to the British North America Act.
Especially are constitutional checks and balances essential where large areas and populations are concerned. Especially is it necessary to have constitutional checks and balances in Canada. Each dominion of the British empire struggled for sovereign power to enable it successfully to resist the efforts of any central government to oppress it. In the United States, the states sternly defend state rights, to enable them to force the central government to give them something like justice.
On the other hand every enlightened person also knows that successful human achievement depends upon co-operation among men. Every enlightened person knows, too, that men are prone to refuse to co-operate even when they have the opportunity so to do, and even when co-operation would be in their own best interests.
That is granted. I am fully aware of that. So were the fathers of confederation. So were the designers of the United States constitution. So were the designers of the British constitution, unwritten but fully understood. If the states of the United States have too much power, they might easily disrupt the union. If they have too little power, the union might easily disrupt them. Those who are thoroughly familiar with conditions in the United States know how tragically the central power in the union has disrupted a large area of the United States.
In Canada the central power in the union has disrupted the provinces, particularly as to their economic lives. The union is not attempting to change policies that have injured the provinces. I ask all hon. members of the Liberal party to bear that in mind, and challenge that statement if they think they can. There is no indication that the federal government is contemplating salutary changes of policies. Rather the indications so far are that the federal government is planning policies even more harmful to the provincial economy. Under existing circumstances, only greater provincial power has any chance of warding off most serious injuries with yet more serious consequences.
I know it can be argued that if you once give Ottawa absolute control over every province in Canada there will never be any breaking away by any province. I am quite agreed as to that. There has been no breaking away of the southern states from the central body in the United States. But what has happened to the southern states? What has happened to their lives? What has produced the share-croppers there? Do any hon. members want to see a lot of share-croppers in the

British North America Act various provinces of Canada? That would be a mighty easy thing to bring about in this country right now; much progress has been made in that direction already in many of the provinces.
The first question to be considered is this: Are strong provincial governments essential to a prosperous and powerful Canada? I maintain that strong provincial governments are essential to a prosperous and powerful Canada. Quebec will insist upon constitutional powers and authority to guarantee her discretion in matters of language and education. Hon. members will notice that this measure is carefully worded to disarm Quebec. The rest of the provinces presumably do not matter so long as Quebec supports the government. As long as Ontario has provincial leaders of sufficient experience and courage, she will equally insist upon the same discretionary sovereignty to safeguard language and education in Ontario, as well as property and civil rights. British Columbia, Nova Scotia, Alberta and the others ought to, and must, have similar powers of discretion to safeguard property and civil rights against the injurious incidence of federal policies, particularly federal policies as regards freight rates, tariffs, finance, land settlement and immigration, and industrial development which up to the present time has been unduly concentrated in Ontario and Quebec.
I am tempted to make a brief aside here and draw the attention of all hon. members and the people of the country to the fact that during the recent war, when there was an admirable opportunity to decentralize industry, very little decentralization took place. The impression we all got was that as soon as the war was over the government took pains to destroy what little decentralization had taken place. In other words, all the new industries were placed right here in Ontario and Quebec. From the standpoint of the other eight provinces, this was most disastrous. Anyone who is well informed on the question knows that.
What are the provinces going to do about the matter? What recourse have the mari-times and the four western provinces, other than increased constitutional guarantees of provincial discretionary power and authority? All any hon. member needs to do in order to get plenty of evidence to support what I am saying is to read the submissions made by those provinces to the Rowell-Sirois commission. I think anyone who reads those submissions will come away a sadder and wiser man. What can be thought of a federally supported and imposed freight rate structure which permits any railroad to charge $1.75 per hundredweight for moving flannelette
[Mr. Blackmore.l
blankets from eastern Canada to Vancouver, for example, and to change $4,534 per hundredweight to move them to Edmonton, a shorter haul by more than 500 miles?
Let it be borne in mind that these inequities in freight rates have to do with railways over which the central government has had and still has absolute control. Hon. members who did not hear me speak on October 24, as reported on page 1090 of Hansard, I believe would be well advised to read that speech- not because of any particular quality of its own, but because of the astonishing things that are in it.

I hear some silly laughter. Some people would laugh if they saw their mothers being killed. Inequities almost as glaring and hurtful to provincial economy can be cited in relation to federal policies in each of the important fields of tariff, finance, land settlement, immigration-think of the Japanese problem in British Columbia-and industrial development which has centralized industry in Ontario and Quebec, and incidentally centralized power there. It may be argued that if more power were concentrated in Ottawa, the federal government would clear away those inequities; but the fact is that Ottawa has absolute power over each of those aspects of national life, and yet flagrant inequities have developed right under the nose of Ottawa, and perhaps with the consent and connivance of Ottawa.
Again I ask: what possible recourse has any province, western or maritime? In this house Ontario and Quebec can outvote all the other eight provinces put together. In his speech the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made a good deal of the privilege the provinces would have of sending members to the house to protect their interests, but what chance would 106 members from eight provinces have of standing up and asserting their rights against 156 members from Ontario and Quebec? I have no feeling of unkindness toward the provinces of Ontario and Quebec; I am merely pointing out the situation which exists and which constitutes one of the facts that enter into this whole matter. I repeat that Ontario and Quebec can outvote by fifty votes all the other provinces put together.
Anyone who supposes that this fact has not had an injurious effect on the other provinces just has not learned anything yet. Unless tremendous industrial development can be stimulated in the western and maritime provinces, the population growth of those provinces will never give the eight provinces enough members in Ottawa to enable them to

demand and obtain the simple human privilege of plain and obvious economic equity.
I make that statement without fear of successful contradiction.
The conclusion is irresistible. Canada is made up of vast areas, and widely varying territories and conditions. If Canada is to become prosperous and powerful, the provincial governments must have constitutional guarantees of essential discretion.
The Prime Minister has iterated and reiterated since September 14, and he stated it before, that there was no desire or intention to impair the safeguards of provincial rights and jurisdiction. These words are extracted from the letter of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), dated September 14, 1949, to each of the provincial premiers, which is to be found at page 870 of Hansard.
The declaration of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) should be weighed and assessed in the light of several relative considerations. First of all what has been the tendency of the Liberal party as a whole in Canada in the last fourteen years? Has its tendency been (a) towards decentralization of power in Canada and in the world; (b) towards maintaining the status quo in Canada and in the world; or (c) towards centralization of power in Canada and in the world? There is no question that the Liberal party has definitely worked towards centralizing power both in the world and in Canada. That cannot possibly be questioned.
Let us first look at the matter from the point of view of Canada. May I draw the attention of hon. members to a document entitled "Proposals of the government of Canada", dated August, 1945, which was submitted to the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction. I should like to read four short extracts from page 48 and page 49 of that publication. They are:
The dominion government proposes that after the war the provincial governments should by agreement forego the imposition of personal income taxes, corporation taxes and succession duties, leaving to the dominion government the full and exclusive access to these revenue sources.
May I comment on that statement by saying that if such a policy were implemented it would mean that the financial and economic independence of every province in Canada would be utterly destroyed. Every province would completely lose discretion in any matter, except under the direction and guidance and at the will and with the consent of the central government. No check would exist in Canada as far as provincial governments were concerned. I continue to read: . . . the dominion proposes an agreement under which the provincial governments would commit themselves not to withdraw before an initial trial period of say three years.
It will clearly need to make full use of its power-
British North America Act
Meaning the dominion government.
-to impose national taxes on personal incomes, corporations and estates.
Exclusive jurisdiction over taxes on incomes, corporations and estates is also necessary in order to protect Canadian interests abroad.
There is the attitude of the Liberal government in 1945. Does it indicate any desire on the part of the government to include "the fullest safeguards of provincial rights and jurisdiction", as related to the allimportant class 13 of section 92, "property and civil rights in the provinces?" May I pause a moment to point out that although there are several important instances under section 91 where the dominion has overriding power, there is only one class in section 92 which gives the provinces any chance in the world to stand up to the dominion, and that is class 13. Just look at the attempts to invade class 13 as indicated in the four proposals I have read!
Will the Prime Minister repudiate the pronouncements at pages 48 and 49 of the documented proposals of the Dominion of Canada? Let him rise in this house and tell us whether he repudiates the statements contained in that document.
Will the Liberal party repudiate them? We have quite a number of Liberals in the house. Will they repudiate these statements? Will the Liberal machine outside the house and the visible and invisible forces that control that machine, repudiate these statements?

It is easy to laugh it off, but it is a grave reality. Let no member of the Liberal party pretend that there are not hidden forces governing the Liberal machine.
Satisfactory answers to each of these questions ought to be forthcoming. Such answers ought to be demanded by all Canadians as a solemn and binding commitment. Until such repudiation and commitment are in our hands how can anyone rely upon the Prime Minister's declarations and his protestations of a desire to "include the fullest safeguards of provincial rights and jurisdiction"? There is an old saying that actions speak louder than words.
The document from which I have just quoted indicates the Liberal attitude four years ago. Have we any documents prior to that time? May I recall to the minds of hon. members the report of the Rowell-Sirois commission on dominion-provincial relations? The commission was appointed by a Liberal administration-and was probably told pretty well what it was expected to do! It was appointed by order in council on August 14, 1937, and submitted its report on May 3, 1940.

British North America Act The dominion-provincial conference to consider the report was called on January 14, 1941.
The documented proposals of the government of Canada of August, 1945, are founded on the gist of the financial proposals of the Rowell-Sirois commission.
Does anyone question that statement? Let me read from an article in Canadian Business of January, 1941, on the Rowell-Sirois report. The article reads:
Plan 1 provides that the provinces would cease to use the following forms of taxation, the personal income tax, corporation taxes, succession duties.
There is an asterisk beside corporation taxes referring one to a footnote which reads:
The dominion would pay annually to each province a sum equal to the tax which that province would have received had it collected from mining and oil producing companies, 10 per cent of the net income which was derived from mining, smelting and refining of ores and oils produced in the province.
It sounds surprisingly like the proposals of the dominion government to which I referred, does it not? Then the article goes on to deal with what the new grants are and reads:
Plan 1 provides that:
(a)	the provinces would surrender all existing subsidies;
(b)	the dominion would pay annually a national adjustment grant according to need, which would be irreducible, but revisable every five years on the recommendation of an independent advisory finance commission.
You can be very sure the "finance commission" would be appointed by the federal government and would consist of men who were ready to do the will of that government. I continue to read:
(c)	The dominion would provide emergency grants in dealing with abnormal conditions subject to the recommendation of the finance commission, which grants would be made for a year at a time only and reduced or suspended as soon as conditions justified it.
I should like to draw from a statement to be found further on in the same article, which I think will impress every hon. member of the house. The article sets out what the adjustment grants were for the various provinces. Prince Edward Island was to have a national adjustment grant of $750,000. Nova Scotia was to have $800,000; New Brunswick, $1,500,000; Quebec, $8 million; Manitoba, $2,100,000; Saskatchewan, 1939 basis, $1,750,000, and Ontario nothing, Alberta nothing, and British Columbia nothing. That does not sound like very good reading, does it? That is what was recommended by the Rowell-Sirois commission, and apparently with the complete consent and approval of the Liberal government.
[Mr. Blackmore.l
Did the Rowell-Sirois report advocate centralization? Here is what some of the grand old Liberals of earlier days said; I quote from an article by W. R. Motherwell, a fact-facing article, written on January 14, 1941, and appearing in the January 23 issue of the Western Producer.
Perhaps some of the younger members of this house may not remember who this man was. He was a grand old Liberal reformer from the west, premier of Saskatchewan for a good many years, Minister of Agriculture in the federal cabinet at Ottawa for a number of years, one of the finest men I ever met and one of the clearest thinkers. He was a Liberal. He was honest in stating what he believed and could give very good reasons for so believing. Listen to what he said concerning the Sirois report.
In view of this, why should we now relinquish voluntarily, some of our present sovereign provincial authority, to build up a still more dominating central power, sometimes even now, not exercised too wisely or too well.
There can be no doubt about what he thought. Further on in the article he said:
Then why, I repeat, should we now increase the further centralization of power in Ottawa (except for increasing our war effort) when they seem to have, or to take, more power than they can administer wisely and well as in the above cited cases, which should, in my humble estimation, be remedied forthwith.
Between those two statements he had listed a number of flagrant cases of mismanagement by the federal government in handling power; and no man was in a better position to know about some of those cases of mismanagement than was Hon. W. R. Motherwell.
The whole Sirois report indicates the trend towards centralization that has consistently characterized the Liberal party since at least as far back as 1937, when the Sirois commission was appointed. Many other illustrations might be given to show that the Liberal party is a party of centralization. What did the Liberal party do with Pattullo and Hepburn, the premiers of British Columbia and Ontario respectively, because they had the courage to combine with Premier Aberhart of Alberta to wreck the dominion-provincial conference in January, 1941? They were not the only premiers who were opposed to the Sirois report, as I could show by a number of quotations; but they were the men who stood out and had courage to do the thing that had to be done. What did the Liberal party do then? They put Pattullo into oblivion. Where did Hepburn go? It may be said that he retired because of ill health. Well, almost anyone would have ill health after the kind of treatment the Liberals mete out to any man who does not do just what they tell him to do.

Now we have evidence enough to warn us what to expect or suspect in any leader of the present Liberal party in Canada, not judging from what they say, but judging from what they have done.
Is the manoeuvre with which we are now faced, of making a request to the British government, merely a trick to achieve by devious means what the Liberals have failed to achieve by less devious means over the last fourteen years? The suggestion deserves serious attention. What are the possibilities, in case the people who are behind the throne of the Liberal party do mean to centralize power, as I do not doubt?
The proposed measure is more than an amendment of the British North America Act. It constitutes a revolution; it means the utter wrecking of the British North America Act. Anyone who believes otherwise is simply leaving out of consideration many important factors.
What gives permanence and stability to the British North America Act as we know it today? It is the fact that the act was passed by the British parliament. That is the hinge on which it hangs. We have had arguments back and forth as to whether the act is a pact or a statute. However you look at it, the act is given stability by the fact that it is a statute of the British parliament. Is that not so?
If the governments of the provinces met together in a constitutional convention and drafted resolutions they all accepted, and which the people of Canada accepted, you would be able to hang the British North America Act on the hinge of the decisions of that constitutional convention. But no provision has been made for calling such a convention. It is not to be done; it is not proposed. Consequently when this address is acted upon by the British parliament the hinge of the present British North America Act, the anchor or mooring, so to speak, will be swept away and the British North America Act will become a ship adrift. Let us be sure that we are fully aware of that fact. There will be no anchor for it. There will be no appeal to the privy council; that will have been abolished. There will be no appeal to the United Kingdom parliament, because that will have been abolished. There will be no constitutional convention to provide anything in Canada upon which the British North America Act can be hinged. Then can anyone tell me what will be the anchor of the British North America Act? The federal government will be in supreme control with potentially unlimited powers, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Vancou-ver-Quadra (Mr. Green). Why? Because no plan will have been prepared for a new

British North America Act Canadian constitution. The provinces will desire a constitution that will genuinely establish and adequately safeguard provincial rights and jurisdiction. The nation could be plunged into a state bordering upon the chaotic, for no one should imagine that after taking this step the Canadian government intends to give the provinces the sort of thing the provinces want and must have. This government will probably come before the provinces in a convention and say, "Now, boys, it is this-or else!" A state of emergency will then have come into being.
Then what? Will not the federal government invoke the peace, order and good government clause of section 91 to deal with the situation? In order to gain some idea of the sort of thing that is in the minds of some of the men who are drafting Liberal party policy I suggest that hon. members take the proposals of the government of Canada from which I read a short time ago and turn to page 10, in the latter part of the first column and the first part of the second column, where we find clearly indicated just the sort of thing that would be contemplated. I have not time to read the passage; I shall have to leave it for hon. members to read for themselves. Would not this move give the federal government plausible arguments for a policy to "displace the authority of the provinces in relation to a vast field in which the provinces would otherwise have exclusive jurisdiction?" I refer to a statement by Lord Haldane, bearing upon a certain judgment. I quote again from page 10:
The overriding powers enumerated in section 91, as well as the general words at the commencement of the section, may then become applicable to new and special aspects which they cover, of subjects assigned otherwise exclusively to the provinces.
There are very few fields of exclusive provincial jurisdiction at the present time. If the dominion government were to invoke that clause contained in section 91, no provincial rights would remain inviolate.
No sane man would ever demolish his house before he had another to replace it. The nation's house is its constitution. No sane nation would contemplate wrecking its constitution before making sure it had another to replace it. That is the solemn fact which faces us.
What is the nature of the change proposed for the British North America Act? If we read section 91, and connect up the passage preceding where this clause is to fit in with what follows, we shall see quite clearly that when I say the dominion government would be given absolute power by the adoption of this address, I am speaking with complete moderation.

British North America Act
What are "the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces"? Anyone who will read section 91 of the British North America Act will discover that it contains many responsibilities, things that cost money, things that are a lot of trouble to administer, but no power in any one of them. There is no assurance of financial means by which to discharge those responsibilities.
As I have said, only one clause, clause No. 13, gives the provinces even a vestige of effective power in asserting those rights, and that clause has to do with property and civil rights. I have indicated already that the invasion of the fields of corporation taxes, personal income taxes and succession duties, virtually destroys the effectiveness of that power. How can a province assert any control over property and civil rights when it has no authority over the taxing power? The central government could pass laws affecting bus lines or trucking companies for example in a province that would make it impossible for them to successfully compete with the railroads. There is nothing to prevent that.
