Anyone is free to draw his own conclusions. After listening to the debate on this question, I have every reason for drawing my own deductions.
The motion before the house, then, concerns the securing of authority to change our constitution or, as the member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) has said, practically throwing away the British North America Act. When one considers this in conjunction with other legislation, namely the abolition of the right of appeal to the privy council, one asks the question, Why? It is simply because this government, or at least some of the members of it, have outgrown their British commonwealth pants and now wish to strut around with their thumbs in their vests, declaring to this country that we are old enough and big enough to carry on our own business. Perhaps that may be true. They have a perfect right to those thoughts. But beneath it all there is one determination and there is a submerged and real danger in it for the provinces of Canada.
The present Liberal government have been returned to power with a large majority. They have a mandate from the people; this large majority gives them that mandate. I hope that it has not awakened in their minds the unholy desire for centralized power and control at Ottawa to the detriment of the provinces, both from a political point of view and otherwise. I also hope that this determination to scrap the last vestige of a tie with the mother country will not result in the passing or the endeavour to pass this motion.
Each of us must think in terms of his own province and what it would mean. The Liberal party at the present time appear to have made up their minds to get a still stronger stranglehold on the provinces and on the affairs of each individual, as it were, so they can dictate provincially, without the possibility of a come-back from any of the provinces; because they do not intend at the present time to ask their advice with regard to changes that are to be made.
45781-76J
British North America Act
As I see it, the picture is this. We seem to be heading straight for a soviet Canada; it looks as if we want to sovietize Canada. It is not far off if we continue to bring in legislation of this kind, whereby an election need only be held at the will of the government in power which can practically control things and tell people how, when, and why they should vote. All this can be looked upon as probable, having regard to the undue haste to get this legislation through. It is not what they are really wanting at the present time. It is only that they must have power, more power and still more power, control, and centralization of everything at Ottawa.
Canada has already obtained its independence. This fact is recognized by everybody. But with this independence, is it Canada's desire to break off all connections with the British commonwealth of nations? I do not believe that the citizens of this country have that desire. There is, however, something else we should consider in connection with this matter. We must look to the future. Canada occupies a unique position, being the connecting link with Britain and with western Europe and, through Britain and western Europe, with the United States. That position must be preserved. While we may have the right to sever the link, why do it at the present time? I would ask the Prime Minister that question.
Through the administration of justice lies the hope for the future. Justice is our common bond with all nations. Prince Edward Island, the cradle of confederation, did not join the union in 1867 or, as it is sometimes called, the pact or agreement; but it matters not what you call it. There was a three-cornered pact anyhow between the provinces, the dominion as it was formed, and the mother country. We did not join in 1867 because the terms offered to us were not considered to be satisfactory. However, we could not be coerced to join because the power to deal with the matter was left to the legislature of our own province. But in 1873, after being wooed by the other provinces, and after better terms were granted, our province entered the union. When we entered it, our province knew that they would have the protection of the terms of the British North America Act in case of non-fulfilment in a large degree of the terms under which they entered confederation. Now all this will be done away with if this motion passes and if the ideas in passing it are carried into effect.
On Monday last we all listened to an address given in this chamber by the Prime Minister of India. Let us take a lesson from India. I think the example set by India ought

British* North America Act not to be overlooked. India was granted complete independence a little over a year ago and is now what might be termed a republic. Yet the right of appeal to the privy council would seem not to be done away with. If this is so, is it not a tribute to the value of the relationship that still exists?
I know that if the celebrated lawyers in this house would look up their weekly notes for the month of August, they would find a summary of an important case that India appealed to the British commonwealth of nations.
The passing of this motion in an arbitrary way, without the consent of the legislatures of the ten provinces, opens the door to the removal of many of the rights of minorities which the British North America Act seeks to guard.
At the present time Britain is experiencing hard going. This hard going is the result of her stand in the last war. She is fighting for her very existence today. A move at this time to further separate this country from Britain will no doubt be interpreted as a break in the solidarity of the British commonwealth, which will no doubt give pleasure to some places and to some individuals.
This is so great a departure from our present system that the whole question should be given a great deal of study, and time should be given for consideration. The question is not one on which all people can make a hasty decision such as we are asked to make at this time.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I am not going to make any extended remarks. In closing I just wish to say through you, sir, to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that the motion will carry, as he knows, because of the rubber-stamp voting power; but with the weight of argument clearly shown by former speakers in this house and the precedents established by Canada's builders of the past and the agreement of the three parties to the contract this motion should be delayed in order that all parties to our confederation may have a voice in the matter. Then when you decide to put this motion before all parties to the contract you will know that democracy will reconfederate Canada.
Again, should this motion be adopted, giving the government the power to amend its own constitution, without consulting the provinces, one hates to anticipate what the future may evolve. I should like to suggest that should this motion carry the opposition should bring in a minority report in the form of an address to His Majesty the King so that the rights of the provinces of Canada will be given back to them and not destroyed.
[Mr. McLure.l

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that in approaching this subject, and in discussing it in the house, some hon. members have put on 1949 glasses when they should look at the constitution through 1867 glasses, and that hon. members are approaching this subject with what they would hope to see in the constitution rather than what is actually in it.
The other day the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) cited some of the remarks I made in a speech in Montreal. From them he gathered that there was a division in the cabinet on this matter, and that the government should proceed cautiously. From my remarks I think hon. members will see that there is no division in the cabinet on the matter. The hon. member for Broadview was referring to a speech that I made in Montreal. Curiously enough the words that he attributes to me were cited from an English newspaper of Montreal and were placed in quotation marks. On that occasion I had no written speech. I had only notes, and the remarks I gave were in French, so I do not see how people could quote me the way they did. In this speech I am reported as having said that Mr. Duplessis is fond of grandiloquent speeches. I do not remember using those exact words, but if I did not I should have.
In that speech reference was made to another speech that had been made by the premier of Quebec in which he recalled to memory what the St. Eustache patriots did in 1837 to obtain a responsible government; also another event of 1841. What I said on that occasion in reference to the patriots of 1837 was that they did fight for the recognition of responsible government, and they also asked the right, the sacred right as a matter of fact, to choose their own representatives. I added to that and said that on June 27 the people of all Canada did the same thing as the patriots of 1837, and chose the representatives they wanted to represent them in the federal house for the next four years. I said further that the people from the various provinces, and particularly from the province of Quebec, having elected Liberal members to represent them, one would not expect that these same members would be treated as strangers when they go back to their own province as we have been by the premier of Quebec.
In that same speech Mr. Duplessis said that in 1867 representatives of the provinces of Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia got together to discuss the constitutional problems.
What I said was that there was no province of Quebec at that time and there was no province of Ontario. There was only one

province of Canada, and the provinces had been created by the Constitutional Act. On that occasion I cited a friend of Mr. Duplessis, Sir Thomas Chapais, who had this to say on the constitution of the provinces.
(Translation):
I quote from Thomas Chapais' "Cours d'histoire du Canada", volume 8, page 213:
. . . especially that part of confederation which affects more particularly the French-Canadian group. We owe them (the fathers of confederation) a debt of gratitude for creating-in the welter of conflicting interests and the intricacies of constitutional problems-a little homeland, the province of Quebec, so dear to us, to which they have given such vitality. Indeed, as far as what was known as Lower Canada, their main achievement is the establishment of a provincial state, of a legislature that is truly ours, where we are the guardians of our closest interests. We have thus been able to achieve an end which the French-Canadian group had struggled to attain, for a whole century, amidst innumerable perils and dangers.
Taking Sir Thomas Chapais as authority, I showed that neither the province of Quebec as such, nor the province of Ontario as such existed in 1867, and that it was only through the enactment of the British North America Act that they came into being.
(Text):
Mr. Duplessis went on to say that the provinces retained to themselves the full authority to deal with matters pertaining to the protection of their rights and privileges. As a matter of fact, as I have just said, the provinces did not exist at that time; therefore they could not have agreed, and they could not have given or retained any powers whatsoever. Mr. Duplessis said: "It was a compact." He went a little further than that. He said: "It was a notarial act." On that occasion I said: "If it was a notarial act he should produce it." As to the matter of a compact or a contract I shall come back to that in a moment. Mr. Duplessis said: "It was a compact that could not be changed without the full consent of the parties concerned." I shall also deal with that a little later.
The premier expressed fear that changes in the constitution, as advocated by the Liberals at Ottawa, might reduce provincial autonomy. I have emphasized the point, and I do so again, that in the motion before the house there is not one iota of a change in so far as rights and privileges of provinces or of minorities or of religion or what-have-you are concerned. We are endeavouring only to find a procedure whereby in Canada we shall be able to do what is done at the present time in London. We have no intention of changing by one iota the rights that are contained in the constitution at the present time. We wish
27, 1949
British North America Act only to add to the constitution machinery of procedure whereby, if at some time in the future there is any necessity to amend the British North America Act, it will be found there instead of being absent from the text.
This brings me to the other remark made by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). I am supposed to have said that "This-extending the French language to all Canada-will be done when the constitution is amended", the reference being to section 133. I did not say anything about amending section 133. I drew the attention of the population of Quebec to the fact that section 133 protected the French language in the federal government at Ottawa, in the federal courts and in the province of Quebec. There is no guarantee under section 133 for the use of the French language elsewhere than in Quebec and Ottawa. I said that it could not be claimed that Canada is a bilingual country. I said also that I would fight in the future- not at this time, because no change is contemplated in section 133-to have Canada known as a bilingual country and to have section 133 amended if necessary so that the French and English languages would be official throughout Canada.
Then a word with regard to the extension of social security benefits, which was referred to also by the hon. member for Broadview. All I said was that I did not recognize the right of the premier of Quebec to use the allowances paid by the federal government to the children of Quebec to buy schoolbooks which up to then had been furnished gratuitously by a Liberal government.
We have to go back to 1837, 1840, 1864 and 1867 to find out what the real spirit of the constitution was. Mr. Duplessis said: (Translation):
We need a strong confederation based on the spirit that inspired the confederation pact.
(Text):
I was asking what spirit had guided the fathers of confederation when they adopted their resolutions. Mr. Duplessis said that the fathers of confederation would never have consented to the subordination of the French Canadian people under a law which could be changed at any time. I am not attempting to say today what might have happened at that time if those people had had such a thought. I can only point out what in reality they have put it in the agreement and in the law. Mr. Duplessis said that it would be impossible for them to survive if the legislature disappeared. There is no intention to have the legislature disappear. On the contrary, we are seeking to create a procedure, or to have the provinces agree as to what procedure should be followed in connection with questions that concern them. That is the whole question.

British North America Act
What is the spirit and letter of the British North America Act? The preamble of the act is quite illuminating. It reads:
Whereas the provinces of Canada-
It does not read "the provinces of Quebec and Ontario"; it reads "the provinces of Canada". As Mr. Duplessis said, the Union Act of 1840 united the two provinces into one province. The preamble continues:
-Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have expressed their desire to be federally united into one dominion-
I draw the attention of the house to the difference between the French and English versions of that preamble, because this is probably what has brought about the idea of a contract. The French text reads, at least as I find it in Chapais' book: (Translation):
Whereas the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have expressed their desire to enter into a contract for the purpose of forming a federal union which would unite them into one dominion.
(Text):
The English text says that there is a desire to be federally united into one dominion. After the fathers of confederation had expressed their desire the Queen's Most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, granted their request or, at least, the greater part of it. As I said the other day, it is just like a group of students who desired to have a holiday but which could not be enjoyed until the principal of the school said it was all right.
The constitution is divided into a number of sections. The preliminary sections are Nos. 1 to 8. The executive power of the federal government is covered by sections 9 to 16. The legislative power of the dominion is covered by sections 17 to 57. The provincial executive power is covered by sections 58 to 90. The distribution of the legislative powers as between the federal and provincial governments is dealt with in sections 91 to 95. The judicature is dealt with in sections 96 to 101. Then there are sections dealing with revenues and other miscellaneous matters. Those constitute the letter of the constitution.
In 1864 there were two divergent views about what the constitution of Canada should be. It was argued by some that there should be a legislative union, but that argument was put aside because it was felt that a country like Canada with different languages, different religions and different races could not be governed by the one government.
Others wanted omnipotent provincial legislatures, but that was also put aside. The fathers of confederation adopted a middle

course and decided on a federal union with federal and provincial governments. What was the spirit that inspired them at that time? Section 90 reads:
The following provisions of this act respecting the parliament of Canada, namely,-
I drop down a few lines:
-the disallowance of acts-
And again:
-shall extend and apply to the legislatures of the several provinces as if those provisions were here re-enacted and made applicable in terms to the respective provinces and the legislatures thereof, with the substitution of the lieutenant governor of the province for the Governor Generalet cetera. It would appear that in 1867 the fathers of confederation gave to the federal government the power of disallowance of all acts passed by the provinces. The fathers of confederation gave to the federal government a supervisory power over what was to be done by the provinces. That is incorporated in the act of 1867 and has not been changed. It shows what was the intention in the minds of the fathers of confederation. Section 91, as everybody knows, has to do with federal powers. It reads:
It shall be lawful for the queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order, and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces-
Therefore the residuary power is given by the fathers of confederation to the federal government. Section 91 goes on to say:
-and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms in this section, it is hereby declared that (notwithstanding anything in this act) the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated . . .
A list of subjects follows. The third one is the raising of money by any mode or system of taxation. I emphasize the words, "by any mode or system of taxation". On the other hand, section 92 reads:
In each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated; that is to say-
And No. 2 reads:
Direct taxation within the province in order to the raising of a revenue for provincial purposes.
There is some sort of overlapping power as far as direct taxation is concerned. There is no doubt in my mind that both the federal and the provincial governments have the right to tax directly. At this point I should like to cite the case of John Deere Plow v. Wharton as follows:
The form in which provisions in terms overlapping each other have been placed side by side, shews that those who passed the Confederation Act

intended to leave the working out and interpretation of these provisions to practice and to judicial decision.
That is a decision of the privy council. Proceeding with the discussion of the various powers, and having in mind what was said by the members of the privy council in the case of John Deere Plow v. Wharton, I wish to draw the attention of the house to section 96, which reads:
The governor general shall appoint the judges of the superior, district, and county courts in each province, . . .
There again the fathers of confederation decided in 1864 that the judges of all superior courts, all district courts and all county courts should be appointed by the federal government and not by the provinces. Therefore they gave the right to the federal authority to appoint those judges.
When it is pointed out that, according to the decision of the privy council, any interpretation which is not clear should be submitted to the courts, we are faced with the objection that it is advantageous for the federal government to do that because it appoints all the judges. The federal government appoints all the judges because it was sc decided by the fathers of confederation in 1867. When the argument is advanced that we should have federal judges on one side and provincial judges on the other side to decide on some point of the constitution, I say that is impossible. I say there are no such things as federal judges or provincial judges. There is no such thing as a judge with a federal mentality or a judge with a provincial mentality, and if there is any such person should not be allowed to preside in a constitutional case because he has prejudged the case, and that should not be done.
Section 101 reads:
The parliament of Canada may, notwithstanding anything in this act, from time to time, provide for the constitution, maintenance and organization of a general court of appeal for Canada . . .
That is what we have done with our supreme court. I wish to point out, Mr. Speaker, that, whereas in all cases of civil jurisdiction, according to article 92 the power to create civil courts has been given to the provinces, with the judges to be appointed by the federal government, in the case of the Supreme Court of Canada, the general court of appeal for Canada, the maintenance, creation and organization of the courts and the nomination of judges are matters given to the federal authority. I say again this power is according to the spirit of the fathers of confederation when they wrote the constitution.
The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) pointed out another instance which shows what the spirit of the fathers
British North America Act of confederation was. According to section 92, paragraph 10, of the British North America Act, it is sufficient for the parliament of Canada to declare that something is for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces for that matter to fall under federal jurisdiction. That again shows that the fathers of confederation wanted it to be that way. Otherwise they would not have written it the way they did.
Another clause which shows exactly the same trend in their minds is section 118 which reads:
The following sums shall be paid yearly by Canada to the several provinces for the support of their governments and legislatures . . .
According to section 118, the federal government has to pay the provinces for the support of their governments and legislatures the amounts therein enumerated. The provinces were not satisfied with the amounts set out in section 118, and on four or five occasions they asked that they be increased. There again I say that the purpose and spirit of the fathers of confederation is in the act at the present time, and has been there since 1867.
As to amendments, the fathers of confederation after making the various provisions they have made, and that I indicated a moment ago, provided for the amendment of the provincial constitution by the provinces themselves. Therefore they gave some thought at the time to the question of amendments. They did not, however, incorporate in the constitution any provisions as to what was to be the procedure to be followed in the case of amendments. We therefore have to go back to the general law that the authority which is empowered to pass a law also has the power to amend it; and I will go even further than that and say, to put it completely aside. Therefore we have to go back to the imperial parliament in London in order to bring about any amendment to the act. It has been argued that the provinces should be consulted. There again I go back to 1867, 1869 and 1870, and I look at what the fathers of confederation have done. Taking the first two amendments, one of them, if I am not mistaken, dealt with the increase of the subsidies to be paid to the provinces, a purely provincial matter. The fathers of confederation did not go to the provinces to ask for their consent. In the first two amendments the fathers of confederation did not even come before parliament to ask for assent. They acted on their own, as a government. Are we going to accuse the fathers of confederation of having acted contrary to the ideas they had themselves expressed in the constitution, because in 1869 or 1871 they did not seek the consent of the provinces?

British North America Act Are we going to accuse them of attempting to destroy the work they had done in previous years? Why therefore should we be accused today when we do exactly what the fathers of confederation did at that time? Why are we faced with an accusation of that kind, when the fathers of confederation at no time consulted the provinces in regard to any amendment?
Some of the amendments made in later years were opposed by the provinces. Now let us transpose ourselves to London, where the authority for amendment rests. It is the British parliament which has had to decide up to the present how amendments were to be effected. They have decided who had authority to suggest any amendment. One after the other they, have accepted the amendments which have been forwarded after receiving the approval of both houses of this parliament; and they have consistently refused to even consider any amendments suggested by the provincial legislatures. In three or four instances, one concerning British Columbia, two concerning Quebec and I think one having to do with Prince Edward Island, after resolutions were forwarded from this parliament representations were made by the provinces asking that the amendments should not be passed. The imperial government refused to consider those objections, and adopted the resolutions exactly as they had been suggested by this parliament.
What happened in 1943, when there was an amendment of the act which I think had to do with redistribution? On July 22 of that year Mr. Price, speaking in the parliament at Westminster, said:
I entirely endorse what the hon. gentleman has just said, that we ought not to discuss the matter, but I think we ought to ask why a sovereign parliament in one of our great dominions has to be before us at all. I really think it is an anomaly, and, though it may not be possible to get rid of it at this moment, I hope my right hon. friend may be able to give us an assurance that at some future date, as early as possible, it will be got rid of.
Then on July 26, 1943, Mr. Anthony Eden had this to say:
I think it is quite clear to the house that this bill deals with a matter which is entirely within the discretion and judgment of the Canadian legislature. In a sense, therefore, this is a purely formal bill.
Then I come to Mr. Beverley Baxter, for whom I know some of my hon. friends on the other side have great respect. He had this to say:
It should be possible to pass a resolution in both houses here and in Canada that in future any alteration or amendment to the British North America Act should be done solely by the Canadian parliament, that the Canadian parliament should itself make any alteration in the Canadian constitution,

and that this house should forgo forever any further passing of any act or measure affecting any of the dominions.
So I say that as the act stands now, with the meaning that has been given to it by the fathers of confederation, the right to amend the whole constitution rests with London, except in relation to provincial constitutions. As someone has said already, we wish to repatriate the right of amendment; but at the present time we desire to do it only with respect to that portion of the constitution dealing with the federal field. We want the provinces to get together with us, not to examine the rights and privileges of anybody, not to make a new delimitation of the powers or privileges of the federal or provincial governments, but to devise a new procedure. We want to get together and agree if possible on some procedure we can incorporate in our constitution, for our Canadian purposes, so that at some future time we may not have to ask ourselves whether or not it is necessary to get the consent of the provinces to amend our constitution. We want to know what the procedure will be for the future, and we want to discuss it with the provinces on friendly terms. We will agree to give the provinces necessary guarantees, if they want them, in regard to language, religion and education.
So I fail to see how the provinces, or the minorities in the provinces, will be protected any the less by what we are doing than if we did not do it at all. We want an agreement to protect the rights of those minorities. Is the premier of Quebec going to refuse to meet with us and discuss what further security or what other guarantees we can give with respect to provincial rights concerning education, language and religion?

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
The proposed address concerning the amendment of the constitution appears at page 828 of Hansard, but since it is rather lengthy I shall not take time to read it. However, I wish to offer some comment with respect particularly to education and taxation, and to indicate my disapproval of the procedure that has been suggested by the government. In discussing this proposal the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) referred to a statement he made last May:
A method should be worked out to amend our own constitution. It is our intention after the election to consult the provinces as to the method by which amendments to our constitution shall be made.
This government received a mandate to proceed with the question of amending the constitution, but only after consulting the provinces. With that I may be in some measure of agreement. The principle was

approved at a conference in December, 1935, and I should like to bring this to the attention of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. That conference adopted a resolution moved by Hon. L. A. Taschereau, K.C., the then premier and attorney general of the province of Quebec, which emphasized that a method for amending the constitution should be devised by representatives of the dominion and provincial governments before any steps were taken in that direction. According to correspondence between the Prime Minister and the provincial premiers, at least six of the premiers, a majority, disagreed to some extent with the procedure proposed by the government. In the closing part of his letter, the premier of Alberta stated:
We strongly urge that this whole matter be held in abeyance pending the conference which you propose to convene at the close of the present session of parliament. It seems to us that this is the only way in which future conflict can be avoided and the unity of Canada, which we all desire, preserved and strengthened.
I believe that is very important. It is the keynote of the greater part of the correspondence from the various premiers.
I should like to refer particularly, however, to the letter from Premier Campbell of Manitoba, since he is the premier of my native province. This letter is found at page 875 of Hansard and is dated October 6, 1949.
The government of Manitoba would be pleased to discuss with the federal government and the governments of the several provinces the questions mentioned by you at any time and place that is mutually convenient.
Your letter indicates that your government has already decided to ask the United Kingdom parliament to amend the British North America Act so that the parliament of Canada would have authority to amend the constitution of Canada, but only in relation to matters not coming within the jurisdiction of the legislatures of the provinces nor affecting the rights and privileges with respect to education and to the use of the English and French languages. The government of Manitoba feels that there might be differences of opinion as to whether a proposed amendment to the constitution related only to federal matters or affected provincial interests, rights, or jurisdiction. Before agreeing to any specific proposal, therefore, our government will examine carefully the manner in which the provincial position is to be protected.
The main purpose of the conference, as I understand it, would be to try to evolve a method of making, within Canada, amendments to those provisions of the constitution which concern both federal and provincial governments. The government of Manitoba realizes that a conference such as this will be dealing with difficult and complex constitutional problems, and that progress towards a solution of them can be made by representatives of Canada and the provinces meeting together. Our government is therefore of the opinion that a preliminary conference, comprising constitutional experts, though not necessarily limited to them, would be useful in clarifying many of the issues involved.
British North America Act We would consequently welcome the calling of such a preparatory conference, and will be glad to participate in it.
I assume that the Manitoba government will be furnished with an agenda for either the preparatory conference or a dominion-provincial conference in sufficient time to afford us an opportunity of discussing items on the agenda and to enable our representatives to make full preparations.
Yours sincerely,
Douglas Campbell
I believe that clearly sets forth the position of the premier of Manitoba, and the same principle is embodied in the letters from the premiers of the other provinces.
Added to that, the premier made a detailed speech which he delivered in the Manitoba legislature on March 24, 194&, in which he said this was his first full speech on the subject of dominion-provincial relations since occupying his present position. He also says he will deal with the benefits which Manitoba secures from the present agreement between Ottawa and Manitoba as well as criticisms of the agreement. I quote from his speech:
During the depression period of the 1930's, several of the provinces of Canada found it to be impossible to provide for their people.
Further down on this same page, he says:
This situation existed throughout that entire period despite the fact that the government of Manitoba had imposed a level of taxation which was higher than that imposed by any other government in Canada, and despite the fact that the services provided to Manitoba people were at a level much lower than that which would be considered satisfactory under modern conditions.
I turn now to page 8 of the premier's detailed speech.
-it is significant to point out that the two plans which were submitted to the dominion-provincial conference by the province of Ontario recognized this principle explicitly by providing that payments should be made to the provinces in accordance with need.
I believe that is a rather significant statement to be embodied in the speech of the present premier of the province of Manitoba. On page 11 of his speech he states:
The government-
That is the government of Manitoba.
-definitely agrees that a conference should be held as soon as practicable, but, to our mind, the timing of the conference is fundamental, and we are consequently of the view that it should be called immediately after the next dominion election. I am, therefore, prepared to state to the house now that this government will take the initiative in asking that a conference be called as quickly as possible after the dominion election.
In the last paragraph, he says:
-it advocates a procedure for obtaining a still better tax agreement.

speechtext:
That speech is in keeping with the letter he wrote in reply to the letter received from the Prime Minister of Canada.
Speaking of education in the province of Manitoba, it may be realized that approximately seventy-five per cent of the entire cost of education in that province is borne by taxation on real estate. I have been greatly concerned about that matter ever since I was associated with municipal affairs, and have continued to be concerned about it since coming to Ottawa. Under such a system, equality of education is not possible for the youth of this land. Year after year the policy of assessing land which brought in no revenue, and endeavouring to collect taxes from that land, has been followed.

I presume I am quite in order, Mr. Speaker, because this motion distinctly deals with matters between the dominion and provinces; and the municipalities, who are to large degree responsible for education, have no recourse other than through their provincial government.
I am going to give you one concrete example. A school board in Manitoba increased its budget for 1948 by fifty per cent over 1947. That increase of fifty per cent in that budget actually meant an increase of seventy-five per cent on the farm land and other real estate within that consolidated-school area. I suppose that concrete example could be repeated in many places. Not only that, but in that same school area a number of farmers, living along the river bank, on land which was among the highest in assessment, lost three entire crops as a result of floods. One can imagine the position in which it put those people.
Owing to the fact that seventy-five per cent of the cost of education in that province must be borne by real estate it is absolutely


impossible, as I have said, to have equality of education, especially when you compare that with the other provinces. I profess to know something about what has happened in Ontario in the past years. I will repeat what I have said in this house and on the hustings. I know the statement has been disputed on the hustings by people in high office; but, since some of those people are here today, they can deny it if they will. When the leader of the opposition was premier of Ontario and minister of education, the grants to school districts were greatly increased. In some of the more difficult areas these grants were increased to as much as ninety per cent. Imagine what a municipality could do for other services when it was relieved of that proportion of the cost of education? I make that comparison because I think that is something towards which we should be striving.
To me it has been an exceedingly important matter. Last fall at the municipal convention in Manitoba Mr. Morton, the municipal commissioner, pointed out the financial difficulties that many municipalities were getting themselves into. In his speech to that great convention he stated that they were then the sum of $3 million poorer in realizable assets than they were in the year 1945, and that for the immediate past year they had an operating cash deficit of many hundreds of thousands of dollars. That situation has a distinct bearing on the type of education that these people can provide for the youth of the land who happen to live within that province, and I think it is a most important matter.
Then I want to make some reference to an organization known as the Manitoba teachers' federation. Their brief has been endorsed by what is to me the greatest and the most influential organization in Canada, namely, the Canadian Legion. Nobody will dispute what that great organization did throughout the war years in assisting the government of the day in various aspects of the problems which they had before them. First of all, this federation points out:
... a new definition of education which involves the all-round development of the child and an emphasis on citizenship, make the educational perspective of 1867 and a narrow interpretation of the provisions laid down in respect to education in the B.N.A. Act untenable today.
I agree wholeheartedly with that statement and with many others in their presentation. They say:
Migration of population within our country, accelerated immigration as witnessed in the past two years, and an apparent inability on the part of provincial authorities to meet the demands of the situation, accentuate the need for the federal government to study the problem in the interests of the nation as a whole.

They go on to state:
We are faced with a national problem. To the degree that the education of Canadian boys and girls is deficient or insufficient, we reduce the prosperity of our nation and increase the vulnerability of our national security.
Further on they state:
Federal aid for education is a need bom of a shift in taxation. Meeting this need may involve fiscal control-safeguards in the spending of funds from the federal treasury-but not policy control.
They make the point extremely clear that while they must have federal aid in the matter of funds, the policy should remain with the various provinces. They state:
In any plan of federal assistance it would be understood and agreed that the expenditure of funds by the government of Canada would in no way be deemed to confer upon any minister or official of the government of Canada any right of supervision or control over any school or educational institution with respect to which any federal government funds are expended.
Their officials state:
Why should we not match the family allowances with grants to the provinces on a per pupil capita basis earmarked for education and conditional upon the province not reducing its budget for education?
I have pointed out that this suggestion had been endorsed by the Canadian Legion. They had asked for federal grants for education. I am sure nobody will dispute the standing of the Canadian Legion in this great nation of ours.

There is no reason in the world why this government could not let this matter stand in abeyance for a few mon.hs, as they have been asked to do by the majority of the premiers of the provinces of this country. No harm would come of it; on the contrary, I am sure that much good would accrue to the various municipal organizations as well as to the provinces, ultimately bringing about greater equality of education for the youth of this great nation which, by the way, is the greatest asset of any nation at this time. I shall be forced to vo e against this procedure, as it is now proposed, although I believe wholeheartedly in certain amendments to our constitution at this time.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose just before the dinner recess I had begun by saying that I had no intention of quoting anybody, be they great men or otherwise, but that I intended, in laymen's language, to try to find the exact difference between us as to this problem which, in my judgment, is a simple one, and can be put in words of one syllable. I said I had no intention of quoting great men. I hope I am not cynical, but in my judgment the word "great" has been used altogether too loosely.

There is no difficulty in being a so-called great man in an expanding economy or in an expanding geography as, for example, the occupation of the middle and western portions of the United States and Canada. In my time greatness has been exemplified by only three men. Two of them are dead. The direct representative of one of them honoured this chamber by his presence just the other day. The second one died in the achievement of that to which he had devoted his life, and in an endeavour in which he lost his life. The third one is still living. I trust that politics will not find in him the feet of clay which we find in most of these people to whom at one time or another we have attributed greatness. If I were asked to choose the man in the Dominion of Canada who most nearly deserves the right to that appellation I would have only one choice. He is not a statesman; he is not a soldier. I think the greatest man whom Canada has produced was that eminent doctor, Sir William Osier. I say that because we must judge people by their contribution to the world and to humanity, and for that quality of high courage in times of adversity. Therefore I think the men I have mentioned qualify.
I said to you, Mr. Speaker, that I would endeavour to find just where we differ. It is a fact that the trouble in which we now find ourselves arises because the fathers of confederation did not provide us in our constitution with a method of curing the ills which were inherent in it. People much more accustomed to research than I am, and more industrious than I am, tell me that the confederation debates are singularly silent on the subject. One can scarcely believe that was an accident. I do not think the fathers of confederation did not contemplate what would appear after the event as something of great simplicity, namely, a method of amendment. Therefore my conclusion is that perhaps with some deliberateness they omitted mention of the method of amendment in their reported debates, and thought that was one thing that they might just as well leave alone at the moment because they might get into the difficulties which are now apparent in the discussions of the problem which confronts us today.
Just what is our problem? No amendments to the constitution are contemplated at this time. In so far as I have heard or have read, no major changes are necessary. By that I mean division of authority and that kind of thing. A major amendment is necessary in connection with the very matter of amendment itself. Therefore we come down to a simple position of difference. Some of us say that it should not be done without consultation with those authorities who gave us

all of our authority. Whether that was by agreement, pact, treaty or something else, I do not care. From all the speeches to which I have listened I would say that we are very nearly unanimous in the opinion that the constitution of Canada, both dominion and provincial, should be amended by Canadians, and that we should not be put to the necessity of going through certain motions which in these modern days are nothing but motions; in other words, the elimination of the red tape, because that is all it is, in having this sort of thing done.
I am not going to criticize anyone. I am not going to say that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said one thing before the election and now does the other. I express no bad faith in any member who has spoken nor shall I, I hope, in any member who votes on this measure. Coming down to the crux of the problem, the nub-I like that word, and I am sure it is one that has been used quite often by the Prime Minister in practising his profession-we come down to one thing only. We all agree that Canadians should amend their own constitution. We are not agreed as to method. I know that the obvious reply to the things I am saying is that we have debated this matter for eighty-two years. All the major parties-I hope my friends to my left will forgive that expression-

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: Considering where it comes from we will.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
I am sorry, but I did not hear you; perhaps it is just as well. The two major parties, if again I may use that expression without offence, have put themselves on record more than once in favour of the broad principle. Here we are sitting in this House of Commons, some 260 odd-there may be the odd vacant chair, Mr. Speaker, but I cannot see them; from your point of view you may be able to see the odd vacant seat but I cannot see them at the moment-trying to do what? We admit that we are all in favour of the broad principle, and yet we are fighting over matters that in themselves are perhaps of little consequence, but in the sum they add up to what? They add up to one very simple thing; that is, should we consult the other interested parties now or should we move on our own now and consult them at a later date?
That is the only problem before this house at this time. I go back to where I was a moment ago. I realize that someone may say, "Well, if we have been at it for eighty-two years it is time we got some action". There is validity in that argument, but it is immediately answered by the suggestion I offer; that if we have been at it for eighty-two years, another six months is not going to
British North America Act hurt anybody, particularly when we know that immediately after the conclusion of this session the interested parties are going to meet and talk to one another. Then it may be said that because of certain things we have seen in the newspapers there is no object in calling such a conference. In my judgment that argument has no validity whatever. We all know that if we who differ carry on these controversies in the newspapers, as one is being carried on now, it does not help the situation when people get together in order to try to solve their difficulties. So the argument that there is no use doing this thing, having this conference, I discard immediately. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) is not here. I am sure he is better occupied in whatever he is doing than he would be in listening to me, but if he were here I am sure he would be the first to agree that in the history of labour relations, the history of conciliation, everyone starts out by saying, "This is rock bottom, beyond which I will not go". The fellow on the other side says exactly the same thing. But time works wonders, and in time they come together. You may introduce a conciliator or an arbitrator, but in time practically all matters are resolved to the general satisfaction of both sides, and business life goes on in the community. So I hope no one will say that just because A says this is a matter of life and death, and there he is going to stand, he necessarily means that. He is nothing more than a smart David Harum who thinks he is in a horse trade, and he is trying to convey the best possible impression to the audience before the trading really starts. In my judgment that is where we are today.
I had no intention of speaking on this matter this evening. I know everyone says that, Mr. Speaker, but in this case I mean it. I am not suggesting that I have a more exacting conscience than anyone else, but I speak in this simple way tonight after having given the matter my best thought and believing that it is my moral duty to say what I am saying, in an endeavour to preserve the idea of conciliation so that our Canadian way of life may not be subjected to jolts from which the country may suffer for a long time. Even in my time to call a man a compromiser was to insult him. Then we had the expression "the middle of the road", and we thought, "What a weakling. He will not stand by his principles, but goes down the middle of the road. He will compromise with anybody". Today to credit a man with the ability to compromise is to pay him a great compliment. That is one of the changes in the thinking of our people within the last few years. I

British North America Act agree most heartily that to call a man a compromiser is indeed not a reflection upon him but definitely a compliment.
So what is our position now? I have no intention of entering upon any legal discussion, but there is a point that has been bothering me. Once we have stepped into the field we are taking over in this bill, then whether or not we like it or whether or not we know it we are undertaking to define a statute which the privy council has been busy defining ever since 1867. It is so easy to say that we are dealing only with those matters which are not within the jurisdiction of the provinces. To me that means nothing. Perhaps that is an exaggeration, but to me it is not an exact phrase, nor is it an expression which can be accurately interpreted to this House of Commons. With the complexity of our life, business and governmental, new situations are bound to arise from time to time, so you can never put that line down on a piece of paper and say this is it. Someone may say, "Well, now we have the Supreme Court of Canada to determine that line, as in times gone by we have had the privy council." That is not enough. If by our legislation we say that the line goes here, I put it to any lawyer on the opposite side of this house: on what possible ground can the Supreme Court of Canada say the line does not go here? In the matters with which we are attempting to deal, this house is and at all times will be the highest court in the land, and the supreme court might very easily find itself incapable of rectifying something after the event.
Now, why consultation? I am not going to suggest any great scheme to the house. I am not going to say we should follow the United States system, under which two-thirds of the states must ratify any amendment. I have never been greatly interested in any amendment there with the exception of one, the amendment having to do with liquor, because I am always following amendments of that kind. You cannot put down any rule and say, "This is what we should do". That is the purpose of consultation.
Let us look at the matter from its worst aspect. I am not going to advocate anything which will give any province an advantage. Let us assume that, after this conference, the worst happens. The worst can only be that we are back where we are today. Nothing can put us back of that position. Whatever has been achieved up until now is finished business. If the conference is a complete failure, we do not lose anything but merely start from the position in which we are now. I make this statement: Anyone who says that we cannot gain something in the way of

unity or peace, is prejudging the participants in that conference in a way in which he has no right to judge them.
All of us here, certainly those of us in the legal business, have participated in arbitrations and conciliation boards. People sometimes think those boards arrive at some strange decisions. They see that two people go one way and one goes another way. They overlook the fact that in Canada many of these compromise decisions between two great factors in our industrial life are unanimous decisions. I believe the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) will agree with that. Even if two people go one way and one another, we have achieved something, because that is democracy functioning in a proper manner. Broadly speaking, the majority is entitled to rule.
I am not suggesting to a great-I have used the word "great" again and this time very respectfully-constitutional lawyer such as the Prime Minister that it is as simple as I have suggested. Even I, one of the police court variety of lawyers, know that you just cannot go to the ten provinces and say, "Vote, and we will abide by the decision of the majority." Many more considerations enter into the problem. If a meeting with the provinces is held, the worst that can happen is a disagreement. I still have enough faith in humanity and in the people who will be gathered together to believe that, although they may not complete the plan, they are bound to make some progress. At the very worst, Mr. Speaker, they will find their points of disagreement and put a circle around them, so we will all know what the position is.
Coming back to the problem we have to solve.-I am not speaking of rules or words or motions or amendments to the amendment which to me, sir, are the trivia in this whole matter-I am asking what we have to lose by consultation. Eighty-two years have gone, and if it happens to be eighty-two years and six months it will not hurt anybody. By the time you and I, sir, have achieved that age we will wonder why everyone wasted so much time talking about it. I believe there is something to be gained by such a conference. I ask the Prime Minister; if there is something to be gained, why go headlong into this business now when it is bound to make the situation worse? Some provinces will be able to say, "You did not consult us; you bulled your way through because you had the strength." I realize, sir, that is not parliamentary language, but I do think it expresses what will be in the minds of many people who are very keen about the matter of provincial rights.
Provincial rights, sir, were arranged at Quebec and Charlottetown. They came into

our act in 1867. The ordinary man in the street is not bothered much in his business by provincial rights and says, "Why should I be interested in that?" The point I make is this: what was done at that time made a federation. What we do now may improve federation. A failure to have that conference now may not destroy, but may injure the federation in this dominion of Canada which we all love so much.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
The
house, I take it, is about to make its decision, and my remarks will have that fact in mind.
I have no extended remarks to make at this period of the debate.
The debate has been characterized thus far,
I think, by much learning, the product of much research in matters legal, constitutional and historical. I shall confine what I have to say at this stage of the debate to certain matters, and my remarks will not be characterized by the approach of a lawyer. In common with my colleague, the member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), I am trying to think of this problem, not as a lawyer, but as a Canadian who wishes to see, above all else, harmony and unity prevail in Canada.
We have achieved complete unanimity in this debate, sir, in our desire to obtain within Canada the right to amend the constitution in whatever respect may be approved by the Canadian people. As the debate has proceeded, however, it seems to me that the different approaches to the question of the means and method have assumed a depth of cleavage which may be more apparent than real and which is, I think, to be deprecated. It is for that reason that in these few closing remarks I hope, if it lies within me, I may be able to make a conciliatory and reasonable contribution.
In the first place, there is an issue as to Canadian harmony presented by this address. We know quite well, sir, in view of the stated positions of the ten provincial premiers, that at least five of them have openly expressed disapproval of the government's proposed method of meeting the problem of finding a formula for the amendment of the constitution. What they are asking is very simple. They are asking that they be consulted. At the moment, it amounts to that. In the face of that reasonable position on the part of the provincial premiers, surely to press forward now and ignore that request is to invite disharmony and, perhaps, a major showdown in relations between the dominion and the provinces. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that ought to be avoided at any reasonable cost, especially when it appears that that could be accomplished so easily.
British North America Act
Why draw ourselves up now representing the federal authority in a sort of battle array? That is not going to achieve the desired formula for amending the constitution. If a conference is held, the people of Canada will have a full opportunity of judging as to the reasonableness of the position taken by those who participate in that conference representing the dominion and the provinces. The people will be the judges and this parliament,
I submit, will be in an infinitely better position after such a conference to proceed with its part in this enterprise of achieving within Canada the right to amend our own constitution.
The Prime Minister talks about achieving complete autonomy in respect of our relations with Great Britain. Surely these provinces have a right to express in a conference their concern, which honestly and sincerely exists, as to whether the result may not be an interference with their provincial autonomy within the spheres confided to them by the constitution. Why needlessly create national strife within the Canadian family? Surely the Canadian method is a better one than that. Surely the Canadian method is to sit down together as fellow Canadians and to talk over this issue which is of joint concern. That, sir, it seems to me is the issue in regard to national harmony.
The second issue is as to statements made by the Prime Minister preceding the general election. I am not going to labour this point because it has been referred to already. I simply take the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made on the radio on May 19, when he said:
It is our intention, after the election, to consult the provincial governments with a view to working out a method, which will be satisfactory to all Canadians, of amending the constitution in Canada.
The Prime Minister, in the course of one interjection in this debate, has suggested that he had something additional in mind in making that statement, and that he was making an exception as to matters that he says are federal. But the fact of the matter is that he did not mention that reservation. He has referred to his mandate. Part of the mandate he has received certainly was based upon an acceptance, by at least certain portions of the electorate, of his statement that I have just quoted. I am quite sure that we who respect the Prime Minister are justified in urging upon him that he should not leave an undertaking of that kind unfulfilled; because certainly, Mr. Speaker, if words mean anything, those words mean that the provinces were to be consulted before the government addressed itself, after the election, to this question of amendment of the constitution. If there was

British North America Act a reservation in 1he mind of the Prime Minister, he did not state it; and the people of Canada, acting upon the statement that he did make, gave him a mandate in accordance with his statement, not in accordance with any reservations that were in his mind with respect to those matters that he calls federal matters.
The third issue, Mr. Speaker, is this. We who unanimously adopt the view that Canada should have within her own borders the right to amend her constitution must not be guilty of defeating that purpose; and I maintain that the procedure that the government is inviting the house to follow will defeat our purpose. Surely the purpose cannot be simply to segregate certain matters that the Prime Minister refers to as federal matters and say, if we do not go any further, at least that will be something worth while, when the very method that is being followed is one that is going to prejudice, if not doom, any attempt to bring about a comprehensive method of amending the whole constitution. It just means that, if there is not agreement at that dominion-provincial conference that is to follow this session, we shall still have to go to Westminster to obtain amendments with respect to a large area of our constitution.
If there is anything in the Prime Minister's argument-and I do not think there is anything in it-that the fact that it is necessary to go to Westminster is a relic of colonial days or days of our dependency, then what is being done here is to continue that very state of dependency. Surely the sensible objective here, Mr. Speaker, must be a comprehensive formula that will embrace all parts of the constitution; and nothing should be done at this date in seeking some lesser objective-and I am afraid in this respect in a shortsighted way-to prejudice our hope of fulfilling that larger national objective.
In this debate an answer has not yet been given from the government benches to the question why, when our constitution is an entity, an attempt should be made now to break it up or to divide it. We are not making any contribution in this measure to a definition of matters federal. A conference with the provinces would have some hope of bringing about a better definition in that field which in times past has been a field of conflict.
I wish to say one word about the amendments that are before the house. I am not going to spend much time on the position taken by the C.C.F. because we know that their policy all along has been in favour of centralization of more power here in Ottawa. But I point out here that the fact that the C.C.F. can introduce an amendment to the Prime Minister's resolution and that, after

further study, the Prime Minister can find it possible to accept the principle of the amendment, and then in his amendment to the amendment, propose to make some further changes, indicates quite clearly that this subject has not been considered as carefully as it ought to have been considered. There has been too much haste. We shall not achieve that completely adequate consideration in our approach to this important problem unless we do the obvious and reasonable thing, namely, allow this subject a place on the agenda that is to be laid before the dominion-provincial conference.
There is no safeguard in either the amendment of the C.C.F. or the Prime Minister's amendment to the amendment, because they simply leave the position as it is at the present time, on the Prime Minister's own argument, namely that at least in matters outside section 92 of the British North America Act, or those matters that relate peculiarly to the constitution of the provinces, it will continue to rest within the power of parliament-which means simply a majority of the two houses; a majority of one in this house and a majority of one in the other place-to bring about amendments at Westminster. It does not matter that you put up a two-thirds rule in this amendment, as the Prime Minister's amendment to the amendment proposes, because it will still rest, on his argument, within the power of parliament or of a simple majority thereof to ask Westminster to bring about another amendment to the constitution that can overnight wipe out the two-thirds rule that he is speaking of. The Prime Minister says that you have to leave it to the sense of responsibility of parliament not to do that. I cannot quite follow the Prime Minister in his reasoning. He is not prepared to leave there this question as to whether the life of parliament ought to be extended in view of a national emergency. He is not prepared to leave that simply to the good sense of the majority of the house. He wants to create a two-thirds rule there. At the same time he says that good sense will prevent the majority from going some other way. I cannot square these two positions that the Prime Minister takes. It seems to me that they are directly contradictory.
Sir, for the same reason, what is being done here in excepting from the scope of the proposed address matters pertaining to the rights of minorities and provincial rights with reference to education does not safeguard those rights. We need to put those rights on a solid basis of constitutional guarantee. On the Prime Minister's own argument, sir, we are simply leaving these rights

exposed to action on the part of the majority of the two houses of parliament. According to the Prime Minister's argument all Parliament has to do is to pass another address asking for a further amendment to the constitution at Westminster and it will be enacted there, because, he says, these matters such as section 133 assuring language rights are matters that lie within the competence of parliament to pass an address upon, on which Westminster without further question, without any consultation with the provinces, will amend the constitution in the form asked for by this parliament. It seems to me that that answers the negative argument put forward today.
The fact is, as has been said a number of times by those who favour this resolution, that out of the eleven times our constitution has been amended, eight of those amendments have dealt with matters exclusively federal and on every one of those eight occasions there was no consultation with the provinces. That was true whether it was being done by those who were close to confederation, by a parliament that included some of the fathers of confederation themselves, or whether it was done by parliaments made up of various parties down through the years.
In view of that established precedent I submit that if we were now to reverse it we would be bedevilling constitutional matters in this country for a long time to come. It has taken long enough to get to the point where we can discuss ways and means of amending our own constitution here in Canada, but if when we are seeking the power to amend our constitution with respect to federal matters we should do what has never been done before, go to the provinces to get that right, they would insist on telling us how to use that right every time we wanted to use it.


Despite all the pleas that have been made in terms of unity and harmony, despite all the plausible arguments that have been put forward, it seems to me that it is the responsibility of this parliament to pursue the course that has been proposed by the measure now before us. Mr. Speaker, before the question is put, there are several other aspects of this whole situation to which I should like to draw attention because in my judgment they require cautious and appraising attention. This afternoon I went into some detail in respect to certain of these aspects, but there are others I should like to deal with.
I should like to know, and I think the people generally in the country would like to know, why the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) delayed his letter to the provincial premiers until September 14. If the election had occurred on August 27 or even on July 27 there might have been good reason for the delay, but these letters went out on September 14, which was just about two weeks before the measure appeared in the Votes and Proceedings of this house. These letters were sent out during the holiday time when, as is well known, a large number of the provincial cabinet ministers would be absent. It was so late that it was impossible, except with great inconvenience, to call provincial caucuses together to discuss the matter. One would imagine that an address to the British parliament for permission to change the British North America Act was an everyday occurrence. As a matter of fact, I rather fancy, when history is written and appraised, it will be found that the proposed address is one of the most important measures ever put forward in the history of the Dominion of Canada. Possibly it will prove to be the most important, perhaps even more important than the British North America Act itself.
Under these circumstances how can one possibly justify the delay in the sending of the letter of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to the provinces? No answer has been given and no hint that would enable anyone to form a logical conclusion that might justify the action of the Prime Minister.
Here is another aspect of the matter. Why was the Prime Minister's letter of September 14 so absolutely full of inexplicit references and instances of faulty coherence that it would almost defy a commission of Philadelphia lawyers to state what the letter meant? I have not the time nor the opportunity tonight, and I do not believe it is in order, to analyse the letter the Prime Minister sent out, which was written in his office presumably by the best educated men in the Dominion of Canada. In that letter there are errors of coherence for which I believe any high school teacher would pluck a grade 12 student if he wrote an essay in that fashion on any grade 12 examination in Canada. I

British North America Act am prepared to take the letter and proceed with a complete analysis of it to show the truth of what I say, if that is desired. To say that the Prime Minister is not well enough trained in English to write a better letter is simply ridiculous. We are left entirely to the conclusion that he must have prepared the letter, full of inexplicit references and instances of faulty coherence as it is, and therefore with a lack of clarity of meaning, by design. If he did it by design then I must say that the matter is serious enough to occupy the house and the country for some days yet.
There is a third consideration. Why was the measure introduced as an address rather than as a resolution? Hon. members of the house who have been here before know quite well that any measure can be introduced as a resolution. If it is so introduced, hon. members have a chance to ask all manner of questions concerning the purpose of the resolution, the meaning of it and so forth, in committee, but inasmuch as the measure was introduced as an address we have not that opportunity and consequently cannot inform ourselves as people in the high court of parliament should inform themselves before forming a conclusion on a matter of such tremendous portent.
Again, why is the measure brought in now rather than in 1950? Various speakers in the opposition have raised that question time and again, but the Prime Minister has never condescended to attempt to give an answer. It is astonishing that we could not wait until 1950 to introduce the measure. It is a matter that requires careful study. I would say that any justice of the peace or small-town lawyer would take the first opportunity to raise that question. Surely hon. members of the house would be held responsible if they did not raise it. I contend there is no conceivably adequate reason for the speed and the promptness with which the measure has been introduced in the house.
Another consideration is that the requested amendment of the British North America Act presented to the house is not an amendment that even remotely resembles any other amendment ever asked for in Canadian history. All through the debate, Liberal and C.C.F. members have made much of the fact that other amendments have been sought in times past, and some eight of them, if I recall correctly, have been asked for without consulting the premiers of the provinces. All those eight put together are not one-tenth as important as this measure.
I said this afternoon that the measure is not an amendment but is a revolution. The measure proposes to destroy the British North America Act, according to any common-sense


interpretation of the situation. That is a matter that needs to be studied carefully. There is no precedent in Canadian history nor in the history of this parliament for the submission to the British government of such an amendment.
There is another consideration. The federal government has never seriously attempted to employ its power over currency, credit and banking to improve economic conditions in Canada. Such power was specifically given to it by section 91. It has only been used once in a while in Canadian history, and never consistently. It was turned over to the banking concerns and allowed to go at that. That is just neglect of the wonderful power that was given to the federal government under section 91 of the British North America Act. If the federal government had endeavoured to use the credit of Canada as it should have used it through wisely employing its ability to use currency and banking, then I contend that there never would have been any need for the federal government to try to invade the provincial taxation fields of personal income tax, corporation taxes and succession duties.
The whole C.C.F. position, the whole Liberal position, and probably the Conservative position-I hope not but I am afraid so-in respect to these three invasions of provincial rights of taxation has been that it is impossible for the dominion government to get the money otherwise with which to carry out the social service program that the dominion government deems advisable at the present time. Invasions of taxation fields would not be necessary if the dominion government were disposed to use the credit of Canada, because if the dominion government would use the credit of Canada it could easily make what is physically possible financially possible for all Canadians. The extent of the benefits which could be derived from that course of procedure would require hours and hours of discussion to elaborate and clarify. Consequently I shall only mention it in passing. Suffice it to say that during all the long history of Canada the federal government has consistently neglected this most valuable of all the powers given to it under section 91 of the British North America Act.
As I said a moment ago, all the social security measures proposed by the dominion government could be provided without additional taxation, debt or regimentation by the wise use of Canada's credit. All the disabilities now suffered by the provinces with regard to freight rates, tariffs, financial policy, and industrialization could be ameliorated and ultimately removed. All the hardships

occasioned Canadians by reason of the tremendous debts which we have accumulated could probably be abolished in forty years by the wise use of Canada's credit without even noticeably affecting Canadians at all.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members of the house require much more time for discussion, obtaining information, and study of this measure and its implications than we have had up to the present. So also do the provincial cabinets and legislatures, and so do the people of Canada. In order to provide the time and opportunities requisite for adequate study, I believe this measure should be considered in committee of the whole.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low):
That the Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole to consider this resolution.
