Mr. Speaker, I think you and all hon. members will agree that the debate on this resolution has been generally on a pretty high plane and carried on in a dignified manner, as is befitting in a matter of this importance, in spite of the fact that some rather extraordinary speeches have been made today.
There are a few points about which I would like to make the position of the members of our party somewhat clearer.
This resolution has to do with the age-old question of what is the nature of our constitution and what are the rights of the federal authority and of the provincial governments. In that respect there have been, and still are, three theories, each of which has the support of a certain number of members of this house and of Canadians throughout the country. One is that the provinces must agree to all amendments, that this constitution is to be regarded as a contract, no word or comma of which may be changed without the consent of the contracting parties; and it is said in a rather loose way that the contracting parties are the provinces. The amendment moved by the official opposition makes it quite clear that when they say "the provinces" they mean the provincial governments; and that has been the implication of most of the speeches by those opposing the resolution. They have spoken of "the provinces" and in their minds the provinces mean the ten provincial premiers. According to that theory, nothing can be done without consulting these ten premiers.
As to what is meant by consulting them, that too is rather indefinite. When an attempt was made during the last session of the previous parliament to determine whether by consulting the provinces was meant securing their agreement, or in other words to reach the situation where any one of them exercised a veto, that proposition was voted down even by the most enthusiastic proponents of the theory that there should be consultation. However, in spite of the negative vote given at that time, it would seem that several of those who participated in that vote would

British North America Act still like the impression to be conveyed to many that they do mean securing the agreement of the provincial premiers.
The other theory is that parliament is entitled to ask for any kind of amendment without reference in any way whatsoever to the provincial authorities. As a matter of fact that is possibly the technically legal position, but that is not and has never been the position of the party of which I have the honour to be leader at the present time. The position of our party is, and always has been, that at confederation the sovereign powers of the Canadian nation were allocated, part of them to the central parliament and part to the provincial legislatures, with anything unprovided for in that specific allocation left within the general powers of the central parliament; and it has been the view consistently held by the Liberal party that provincial powers should be respected. The corollary of this respect for all the portions of the national sovereignty allocated to the provinces is-our party has contended-that the powers allocated to the central authority can be exercised by that central authority through the members elected by the people to represent them in the central parliament, without any control by the provinces or, I should say, by the premiers of the provincial governments. For a long time, that was the traditional view of the official opposition.
In that respect, I should like to put on record a letter which in its day was confidential but which today forms part of the history of this country and is published with the correspondence of Sir John A. Macdonald. The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) said that the word "great" had been used quite loosely. There are still many of us, even on this side of the house, who do not feel it is used any too loosely when applied to Sir John A. Macdonald.
On the 14th of May, 1886, he wrote to Lieutenant Governor Richey of Nova Scotia the following letter:
Ottawa, 14th May, 1886
My dear Richey:
I see your ministers are going to dissolve.
The permission to grant or refuse a dissolution rests with you, as well as to fix the time for holding the elections. As important issues are, it is said, to go before the people, you should, I think, insist that they should not be taken by surprise and that ample time should be given them for consideration.
Your legislature's legal term of existence expires,
I take it, on the return day of the writs of election, and no election need be held until after that day.
Should your ministers found their advice for an early dissolution, on the ground that they desire an immediate expression of the will of the people as to their remaining in the confederation-you will,
I have no doubt, feel it your duty as a dominion officer, to decline to allow that subject to enter into consideration at all. The representatives of Nova rMr. St. Laurent.!
Scotia as to all questions respecting the relations between the dominion and the provinces sit in the dominion parliament and are the constitutional exponents of the wishes of the people with regard to such relations. The provincial members have their powers restricted to the subjects mentioned in the B.N.A. Act and can go no further. X write you confidentially, but if necessary you will be supported by the whole weight of the dominion government.
Yours sincerely,
John A. Macdonald
I am going to repeat that.
The provincial members-
And that would include the members of the provincial governments.
-have their powers restricted to the subjects mentioned in the B.N.A. Act and can go no further.
When we talk about the provinces in that general way, one would think that we did not mean the group of people inhabiting a certain determined territory but who are, nevertheless, Canadian citizens and are, as such, represented in the Canadian parliament. Those people have as their spokesmen, with respect to those portions of Canadian sovereignty assigned to the central authority, the members they elect to represent them and to speak for them in this house. When we hear the assertion that a letter written by a provincial premier represents the views of four million or more Canadian citizens-well, we are entitled to ask the fifty-seven Liberal members who are here from the province of Ontario if they have anything to say about it.
Forty-five years later, the attitude of those who are now the official opposition, through their spokesmen, was not so much different from that expressed by Sir John A. Macdonald in this letter to the Lieutenant Governor of Nova Scotia. I quote the remarks of Mr. Guthrie, the Minister of Justice in the government headed by the late Viscount Bennett. Speaking in this house on the resolution moved by' Mr. Woodsworth, as reported at page 1473 of 1931 Hansard, Mr. Guthrie said:
However, I agree that the time has come when we should seriously consider this whole question of amendments to the Canadian constitution.
On the next page, 1474, he said:
My contention has always been that in all matters appertaining to the legislative jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada the parliament of Canada has the right, and should have the right expressed, to make such amendments to the constitution as it shall see fit.
That was in 1931. It was a reassertion in which all the members of the Conservative party who were in the house at that time- there were more of them then than there are now-acquiesced. That is what we are proposing to do by this resolution; that and no more. We are proposing to have it expressed

that parliament has the right to make such amendments to the constitution in all matters pertaining to the legislative jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada as it shall see fit.
Now, that being the extent to which we propose to go now, I am met with the charge that I am breaking two pledges, one made in this house I think in February of this year, and the second in a speech made over the radio from Moncton on May 19, 1949. Let us deal with them in chronological order. The pledge was supposed to be contained in the words cited by the leader of the opposition as set out in Hansard at page 962, and are as follows:
The procedure which I believe would be required to deal with a question of the kind would be similar to that which was followed at that time, some twelve or fourteen years ago.
What I said in May has again been cited.
The record of Canadians in two world wars demonstrated beyond any question our ability and our capacity to bear the responsibilities of full nationhood. But our adult nationhood is not yet fully recognized in our constitution and our laws... A method should be worked out to amend our constitution in Canada.
That won't be easy. We do not want the Canadian constitution to be too rigid, but we do want to make sure it contains the fullest safeguards of provincial rights, of the use of the two official languages, and of those other historic rights which are the sacred trusts of our national partnership.
It is our intention, after the election, to consult the provincial governments with a view to working out a method, which will be satisfactory to all Canadians, of amending the constitution in Canada.
The effort is made to interpret that language as a statement that we were abandoning the traditional policy of the Liberal party of dealing, without reference to the provinces, with those matters which by the constitution have been allocated to the central parliament. I never would have given such an undertaking because I feel some responsibility with respect to the future of this country, and I feel that it would be a grave error, at any time, to subject the exercise of the powers given by the constitution to the central authority, represented by the elected representatives of the ten Canadian provinces now, to the control of gentlemen selected to administer those portions of the Canadian sovereignty that have been allocated to the provincial legislatures.
In February of 1949, in this pledge supposed to have been given to the House of Commons, I said the procedure we would follow would be similar to the procedure that had been followed at the time of the 1935 or 1936 dominion-provincial conference. All hon. members know that the recommendation made at that time with respect to amendments with regard to purely federal matters was that they were to be made by simple act
British North America Act of this parliament, and that it was only with respect to matters that were not within the exclusive jurisdiction of this parliament that there was to be another procedure.
Some hon. members have said: But you did not make any restriction. You said you proposed to call a conference of the provinces. We do propose to call a conference of the provinces. The letter read by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) and which, in his view, is so incoherent, is a declaration to the premiers of the provinces that we wish to have a conference with them to deal with those matters which are the ones usually referred to when we speak of substantial amendments to the constitution, namely, those which might effect the transfer of powers from one jurisdiction to the other. But there never was any statement made that there would be no other amendments to the Canadian constitution than those that may be of joint concern to dominion and provincial authorities until we had established a procedure for dealing with that portion of the knotty problem.
One hon. member said: Why go about it in this way? Why do it piecemeal? Perhaps the hon. member who put that question has some friends in the editorial office of the London Free Press. Here is an article from the London Free Press of October 19 which contains this statement:
The government is apparently determined to go ahead with its project of transferring to Ottawa the power to amend those parts of the constitution entirely within federal jurisdiction before calling the conference to decide the method of amending the constitution regarding matters under provincial or mixed jurisdiction.
The hon. member's friend goes on to say:
There is no doubt that this procedure is contrary to logic.
With that statement I do not agree. But he goes on to say:
But it has the advantage of reaching some definite conclusion within a predictable period. With Premier Duplessis clinging stubbornly to the compact theory of confederation, which insists that no jot or tittle of the B.N.A. Act can be changed without the consent of all the provinces, prospects for agreement at any conference are not particularly roseate.
That is why, after eighty-two years of efforts, I ventured to say there might be some Canadians who would prefer to get half a loaf at this time rather than to risk getting nothing at all.
For that I am taken to task by another great newspaper, the Montreal Gazette, which insists that the constitution is being torn into shreds, that it is being torn right down the middle, and that ultimately, when it is hung on the wall, it is going to hang in a crooked

British North America Act fashion because we are grabbing a half loaf before our guests come to the table at which we are inviting them to meet us.
I am not greatly impressed. I have been here now for some time, and I remember many occasions when there have been the loudest of assertions in this house that the aim of the government was good, that what we were proposing to do was all right, but that we were going about it in the wrong fashion. Those who were here in 1946 will remember that everyone just deplored the inequities that had been brought about under the British North America Act with regard to representation of portions of the Canadian public in this House of Commons. Everyone wanted to see that unfair situation remedied. Everyone was convinced that it was conducive to national unity to remove an injustice of that kind. But, it was said, you must not do it until you talk to the premiers; it is all right, as a matter of fact, but you are going about it in the wrong way. Well, we went about it, and it was done; and the representation of the Canadian public in this House of Commons is on a basis fair and equitable to every part of the country.
During the last session when it was suggested that we have this parliament approve the union of Newfoundland with Canada, it was said that that was a grand thing, something that everyone had been in favour of ever since the first days of confederation; it was something that was going to be a grand thing if only it could be done, but you must not do it in that way; that was the wrong way. Again it was said that the right way was to go and talk to the provinces represented by the premiers of the then nine provinces and, if you get their blessing, so much the better; but your chances of getting it did not seem to be good, and you should not endanger national harmony by disregarding the views of those dear provincial premiers who should exercise their control over the manner in which we exercise the powers allocated to this parliament by the constitution. Well, we went ahead; and I am glad to see even members of the opposition from the tenth province of Canada sitting in this House of Commons in this parliament.
Almost immediately after that there was in the house another general expression of opinion by the opposition that since the provincial governments and provincial legislatures did not see fit to take over rent control, it was a good thing to maintain rent control for a further period in the country, but that we were going about it in the wrong way. It was a splendid thing to retain control over steel and over one or two other things but we should not have all that in the same bill.

That was the wrong way to do it. It was said we wanted the thing done but we did not want it done in the way the government was proposing. Well, it was done in the way we were proposing, and an opportunity was given for the Canadian public to say whether we had been proceeding in the right way to do the right things. When I am told again on this occasion that what we are doing is the right thing, but we are doing it in the wrong way, I rather feel that there is a majority of the Canadian people who would like to see it done now, and that is the way we are proposing to do it, and I think that is the way the Canadian people will be glad to see it done.
I wish to state once again that the whole situation is and what we are proposing to do and what we are not proposing to do at the present time. The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) said that it is going to be difficult to get agreement as to where the line is to be drawn between those powers allocated to the central authority and those which were allocated to the provincial authorities. I am in full agreement with him, and do not think that if we had a conference that lasted for twelve months, or if we had twelve conferences that lasted for twelve months each we would get agreement with the provincial premiers as to exactly where that line is to be drawn because, as the hon. member said, the circumstances of the times change the picture in which that line has to appear.
Our proposal is based upon the assumption that there is a line, but that it would not be fair for us to attempt arbitrarily to draw that line. We shall have it declared in general terms, that we have the power, without consulting the provinces as represented by the ten premiers, to deal with those things that are on our side of the line. If, it is felt, we attempt to do anything which anyone feels crosses the line or impinges in any way on something that is outside our jurisdiction, there will be the courts to decide whether we are right or whether we are wrong.
Some hon. gentlemen say that that is not good enough. Well, that is the best that human ingenuity has been able to devise throughout the hundreds and thousands of years that there have been disputes between human beings. The only other way is to resort to arms. Happily for us, the other way, the trial of strength, has long since been abandoned in our domestic affairs.
The moving appeals made to us today, some made before today, in the course of this debate, that we do nothing now, do not create a very profound impression upon me at this time. I was surprised at the different tone used, for instance, by the hon. member for

Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) when we were discussing the previous matter before this house, and when the doctrine of stare decisis was not only sacred but something which had to be written into the statute itself, to find him in this debate not only disregarding the doctrine of stare decisis, which is a doctrine under which a decision is applied to another like case, but disregarding the formal judgment rendered in the very matter that he was discussing, that this parliament has the right, without consulting anybody, to make the Supreme Court of Canada the court of last resort for all Canadians.
There has been not only something which could be invoked as stare decisis, but there is res judicata on that question, and that judgment was rendered after certain provinces, or I should say the representatives of the provincial governments, stated their case before the courts of justice, first of all, before the supreme court and then before that other great court which at the time was the court of last resort. In the heat of argument I think that sometimes rules of logic are forgotten if they do not happen to fit the requirements of the argument that one wishes to make.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext: We have another precedent on that, have we not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY THE KING
speechtext:
There have been many precedents in this debate where the rules of logic were forgotten, and though I cited to the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) an editorial from the London Free Press I do not admit their first assertion that our procedure is devoid of logic. It seems to me that our procedure is quite logical. We say that we wish the right to deal with the Canadian constitution to be here in Canada and to be exercised by Canadians, and everyone says that that is a splendid thing. We say that there are three series of matters which may require amendment from time to time. With respect to one of them the right to deal with such amendments has been in the constitution since 1867. If that piecemeal right to make amendments to the British North America Act means tearing the act in two, well it was torn in two before it was put into the statute book, because when it was put there it was put there with the express provision that all these matters that were of purely provincial concern could be amended by the provincial legislatures without consulting anybody else.
As there are certain matters which are under the exclusive control of the provincial jurisdiction, so there are certain matters that are under the exclusive control of the federal jurisdiction, and there are others which are of joint interest to both, as would necessarily
British North America Act be the transfer of authority from this parliament to a legislature, or from one or more legislatures to this parliament. We say, well, now, before we tackle this difficult problem of getting a procedure agreed upon whereby things that are yours or things that are ours can be transferred from one to the other we shall put ourselves in the same position in which you are. We are not going now to deal with matters with which the provincial authorities have any concern. We are going to get right away for the federal parliament the position the provincial legislatures have had since 1867 with respect to these matters that are of our exclusive concern, and then we shall meet the provincial representatives and shall discuss with them the procedure to be agreed upon by us all as to how we can deal in Canada with the other matters with which they cannot deal under the present subsection 1 of section 92 and which we shall not have the right to deal with under the new subsection 1 of section 91. Until we do reach an agreement we shall still be in the position that, if amendments are required, they will have to be made by the parliament at Westminster. But, up to the present time, of all the amendments that have been made only two were of the character that would in future require a pilgrimage to London. All the others in the nine other cases are matters that Canadians would settle in their Canadian parliament for their Canadian fellow citizens.
It will be much preferable to secure agreement on the method to make the future amendments, and when we do secure that agreement we shall have to make one more pilgrimage to the parliament at Westminster to get that agreement written into the Canadian constitution. That agreement should provide the guarantees that are not there now for provincial jurisdiction, provincial rights, educational rights, language rights, for the right of members of parliament to have at least one session every twelve months, and the right of the electors to pronounce upon the individuals to be their representatives in parliament at least every five years. This resolution will not give those guarantees, but it will not give the parliament of Canada any right to touch any of those entrenched matters. If and when we can get agreement with the provinces we will have one last amendment made by the parliament at Westminster that will truly entrench those rights and provide the best possible safeguards for provincial jurisdiction, provincial autonomy, provincial rights, minority rights and the democratic right of the whole Canadian people to pass from time to time its judgment on those who exercise this sovereign authority.
